Part 1 — Diseases of Immunity 1 (Trans 2.01)

Basic immunity → cells → MHC → cytokines → adaptive response → the four hypersensitivity reactions → immunity in cancer

1. Innate Immunity — the first line of defense

Trans 2.01 p.1–2▸
MUST KNOW Core idea

Innate immunity is present before infection, so it is ready to give instant defense against microbes and to eliminate damaged cells. It works by one three-step logic: recognize → activate → eliminate.

Components of innate immunity

Epithelial barriers
Skin epithelium, GI mucosa and respiratory system are mechanical barriers that physically prevent microbes from entering organ systems.
Neutrophils and monocytes
Once the initial barrier is breached, these phagocytose the microbes. Monocytes are called macrophages when they are found in tissues.
Mast cells
Play a key role in allergic reactions and produce inflammatory mediators.
Dendritic cells
Part of innate immunity and the bridge to adaptive immunity (see Topic 3).
Innate lymphoid cells (NK cells)
Differ from T lymphocytes in only two ways — they do not have T-cell receptors and they do not respond to antigens.
Plasma proteins
Part of the complement system.

Recognition molecules p.1

PAMPsPathogen associated molecular patterns. Structures shared among related microbes that are often necessary for infectivity. Recognized by phagocytic cells such as neutrophils and macrophages.
DAMPsDamage associated molecular patterns. Molecules released by injured and necrotic cells. Also recognized by phagocytic cells.
Pattern recognition receptorsThe receptors that recognize PAMPs and DAMPs. 4 major classes — Toll-like, Nod-like, C-type lectin, Rig-like.

The 4 pattern recognition receptor classes p.2

Comparison table — receptors of innate immunity
ReceptorWhere it sitsWhat it detectsSignaling resultExam clue
Toll-like (TLR)Plasma membrane and endosomal vesiclesBacterial products, microbial polysaccharide, nucleic acids of ingested microbesCytoplasmic TLR → NF-κB (a transcription factor) → synthesis and secretion of cytokines plus expression of adhesion molecules.
Endosomal TLR → interferon regulatory factors → antiviral cytokines.		"Best and most well-known." Two locations, two different outputs.
Nod-like (NLR)CytosolicProducts released from damaged cells and some microbial products (bacterial peptidoglycan)Signals via the inflammasome, a cytosolic multiprotein complex, which activates caspase-1, the enzyme that cleaves the precursor form of IL-1Inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1. IL-1 recruits neutrophils and induces fever.
C-type lectin (CLR)Plasma membrane of macrophages and dendritic cellsFungal glycansElicits inflammatory reactions against fungiLectin = the anti-fungal receptor.
Rig-like (RLR)Cytosol of most cell typesNucleic acids of viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm of infected cellsStimulates production of antiviral cytokinesRIG = the anti-viral cytosolic sensor.
MECHANISM TLR signaling, the two branches
Microbial product binds TLR ├── Cytoplasmic TLR → activation of NF-κB → cytokines + adhesion molecules → recruitment and activation of leukocytes in inflammation └── Endosomal TLR → activated interferon regulatory factors → production of antiviral cytokines (type 1 interferon)

Both cytokines and adhesion molecules are needed for leukocyte recruitment — one alone is not enough.

MUST KNOW Two limitations of innate immunity p.2
  • It is NOT specific. It can only produce inflammation, which is a non-specific reaction, as opposed to producing antibodies.
  • It has no memory. It cannot mount a faster response when it meets the same microbe the second time around.
  • What it does contribute — limited protection against viruses and microbes by inducing inflammation, and more importantly it prompts adaptive immunity to provide robust and better protection.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Innate immunity is present before infection, non-specific, and has no memory.
  • PAMPs come from microbes, DAMPs come from injured and necrotic cells, and both are read by pattern recognition receptors.
  • TLR is the best known — cytoplasmic TLR works through NF-κB, endosomal TLR works through interferon regulatory factors.
  • NLR → inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1, and IL-1 recruits neutrophils and causes fever.
  • CLR = fungi, RLR = cytoplasmic viruses.
  • NK cells are innate lymphoid cells — no TCR and they do not respond to antigens.

2. Adaptive Immunity — cell-mediated vs humoral

Trans 2.01 p.2▸
MUST KNOW Core idea

Adaptive immunity is a learned response and is more potent than innate immunity. It consists of lymphocytes and antibodies and it relies on previous exposure to antigen to provide a specific and strong immune defense.

Cell mediated
  • Mediated by T cell lymphocytes — helper, cytotoxic, regulatory
  • Acts against intracellular microbes and toxins
  • Example given in lecture — cancers
Humoral mediated
  • Mediated by B lymphocytes and their secreted products, called antibodies or immunoglobulins
  • Acts against extracellular microbes and their toxins

The three T cell subsets

Helper T cells
Help B lymphocytes make antibodies and help activate other cells to kill microbes.
Cytotoxic T cells
AKA killer T cells
Kill target cells that bear specific antigens while sparing neighboring uninfected cells.
Regulatory T cells
Regulate the immune response and prevent reaction to autoantigens.
COMMON CONFUSION Intracellular vs extracellular

Cell mediated handles what is inside the cell (intracellular microbes, toxins, cancers). Humoral handles what is outside the cell (extracellular microbes and their toxins). If the target is hiding in the cytoplasm, antibodies cannot reach it, so the T cell must do the job.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Adaptive immunity is learned, specific, more potent, and needs prior antigen exposure.
  • T cells = cell mediated = intracellular. B cells = humoral = extracellular.
  • Helper T helps, cytotoxic T kills, regulatory T prevents reaction to autoantigens.

3. Cells in the Immune System — DC, macrophage, T cell, B cell, NK cell

Named for its fine cytoplasmic processes

T lymphocyte detail — CD4 vs CD8 and activation p.3

CD4 T cells
  • Mainly helper T cells that secrete cytokines and assist macrophages and B cells
  • Recognize antigen on MHC class II
CD8 T cells
  • Mainly cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) that destroy host cells containing microbes
  • Recognize antigen on MHC class I

CD4 and CD8 are expressed on mutually exclusive subsets of αβ T cells — a cell is one or the other, not both.

MECHANISM T cell activation needs two signals
TCR reads antigen–MHC complex+ Co-stimulatory receptor (CD28)→ Full T-cell activation

TCR recognition of the antigen–MHC complex alone is not sufficient for full T-cell activation. Co-stimulatory receptors such as CD28 provide the additional signal. Co-receptors and co-stimulation exist so that T cells are activated appropriately rather than reacting indiscriminately to antigens in the body.

Microscopic morphology p.3

COMMON CONFUSION NK cell vs cytotoxic T cell
NK cell
  • Innate, no TCR, does not respond to antigens
  • Needs no prior sensitization
  • Kills via CD16-mediated ADCC of IgG-coated targets and kills cells lacking MHC I
Cytotoxic T cell
  • Adaptive, has a TCR, antigen specific
  • Needs antigen presented on MHC class I
  • Kills via perforin and granzyme
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Dendritic cell = the antigen-presenting link between innate and adaptive, Langerhans in skin, follicular DC in germinal centers.
  • Macrophage eats what is opsonized by IgG or C3b.
  • TCR recognizes, CD3 and ζ transmit. Activation needs TCR signal plus CD28 co-stimulation.
  • Only plasma cells secrete antibodies. B cell receptor is IgM or IgD, with CD21 for complement and CD40 for helper T signals.
  • NK cell = CD16 → ADCC, secretes IFN-γ, driven by IL-2 and IL-15 for proliferation and IL-12 for killing.
  • Plasma cell morphology — eccentric checkerboard nucleus with a paranuclear hoof.

4. Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC / HLA)

Trans 2.01 p.3–4▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

MHC molecules display peptide fragments of protein antigens for recognition by antigen-specific T cells. The lecture's analogy — MHC is the matchmaker that introduces the correct antigen to the correct T cell. Without MHC, the antigen and the T cell will not meet and cannot get together.

Also known as
Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), because it was first detected in human leukocytes.
Gene location
Genes encoding HLA are clustered on a small segment, the short arm of chromosome 6.
Transplant role
MHC are the genetic products that induce rejection of transplanted organs. The name comes from their role in determining tissue compatibility between individuals.
Polymorphism
Highly polymorphic with thousands of distinct alleles. Everyone's HLA alleles differ from most other individuals, and only identical twins express the same MHC molecules, which is why a transplant match is difficult or nearly impossible to find.
Why variability matters clinically
It explains why some people are susceptible to allergies or autoimmune disease, and why others appear immune or more tolerant to certain microbes.

MHC class I vs class II p.4

Comparison table — the two MHC classes
FeatureMHC Class IMHC Class IIExam clue
Expressed onAll nucleated cells and plateletsMainly antigen-presenting cells — B lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cellsClass I is everywhere, class II is only on APCs
Gene regionClass I MHC molecules regionEncoded within the HLA-D regionD for class II
Peptide sourcePeptides derived from virus / tumor, cytosolic proteins, including some non-pathogenic proteins and tumor-specific antigensAntigens derived from extracellular microbes and soluble proteins after internalization into endosomes or lysosomesClass I = inside the cell. Class II = swallowed from outside
Processing detailCytosolic protein → unfolded → peptides in cytosol → loaded on class I in ERInternalized proteins are digested into peptides then transported to the cell surface as stable peptide–MHC class II complexesEndocytic vesicle is the giveaway for class II
Recognized byCD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes — MHC class I restrictedCD4 helper T lymphocytes — MHC class II restricted1 × 8 = 8 and 2 × 4 = 8
Co-receptor bindingTCR recognizes the MHC I–peptide complex and CD8 binds the heavy chain of MHC class ICD4 acts as the co-receptor for class IICD8 grabs the heavy chain
PurposeEliminate viruses and kill tumor cells. Viral infection and cancer can arise from any nucleated cell, so all nucleated cells express class I and can be surveyed by CD8⁺ T cellsLet cells that have ingested antigens present them and respond to signals from helper T cellsClass I exists everywhere precisely because cancer and virus can start anywhere
Mnemonic (from the PDF) — the product always equals 8

MHC class II binds CD4⁺ T cells → 2 × 4 = 8. MHC class I binds CD8⁺ T cells → 1 × 8 = 8. Both products equal 8, so if your pairing does not multiply to 8, you have swapped them.

MUST KNOW Important to know box from the PDF p.4
  • HLA genes are encoded on Chromosome 6.
  • MHC class I — expressed on all nucleated cells and platelets.
  • MHC class II — expressed mainly on antigen-presenting cells (APCs).

SHOULD KNOW A number of autoimmune and other diseases are associated with the inheritance of particular HLA alleles, a link discovered as early as the 1960s. The lecture also flags active research on CD4 and CD8 T cells in stopping the spread of cancer. p.4

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • MHC = HLA, on the short arm of chromosome 6, highly polymorphic, only identical twins match.
  • Class I on all nucleated cells and platelets → CD8. Class II mainly on APCs → CD4. Product equals 8.
  • Class I peptides come from cytosol / virus / tumor. Class II peptides come from endosomes and lysosomes.
  • MHC differences are the reason transplants are rejected.

5. Cytokines

Trans 2.01 p.4▸
MUST KNOW Core idea

Cells of the immune system communicate with one another through cytokines. They are messengers that are the source of soluble, regulatory signals that initiate and restrict inflammatory responses to pathogens and injury. The group includes interleukins, chemokines, interferons and lymphokines.

  • Their synthesis and release must be highly regulated, sequentially and temporally orchestrated.
  • Controlling cytokines, either by inhibition or by regulating their production, is an approach for controlling the harmful effects of inflammation and tissue-damaging immune reactions.
Table 1 of the PDF — predominant cytokines released during activation of innate and adaptive immunity p.4
Innate immune systemAdaptive immune system
TNF, IL-1, IL-12, type I IFNs, IFN-γ and chemokines
Sources — dendritic cells, macrophages, innate lymphoid cells, NK cells, plus endothelial and epithelial cells		 IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-17, IFN-γ and TGF-β and IL-10
Source — CD4+ cells
EXAM TRAP The overlap cytokine

IFN-γ appears in both columns. Do not use IFN-γ alone to decide innate versus adaptive. The clean innate-only markers in this table are TNF, IL-1, IL-12 and type I IFNs, and the clean adaptive-only ones are IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-17, TGF-β and IL-10.

IL-2Growth factor that stimulates T cell proliferation, increasing the number of antigen-specific lymphocytes. Also stimulates NK cell proliferationCD4+ helper T cells p.4
IL-4Acts on B cells by stimulating IgE class switching and promotes development of additional Th2 cellsType I hypersensitivity p.5
IL-5Activates eosinophilsType I hypersensitivity p.5

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Cytokines are how immune cells talk to each other, and they both initiate and restrict inflammation.
  • IL-1 = neutrophils plus fever. IL-2 = T cell growth. IL-4 = IgE switching plus Th2. IL-5 = eosinophils. IL-12 = NK killing plus IFN-γ. IL-13 = IgE production. IL-17 = neutrophils and monocytes. IFN-γ = macrophage activator.
  • Blocking cytokines is a therapeutic strategy against tissue-damaging inflammation.

6. Adaptive Immune Response — cell-mediated and humoral pathways

Trans 2.01 p.4–5▸

A. Cell-mediated immune response p.4

MECHANISM Cell-mediated response, in order
Antigen presentation by APCs — the dendritic cell binds the antigen and brings it to the lymph node to present it to T lymphocytes ↓ CD4+ helper T cells recognize MHC-associated peptide antigens displayed on DCs ↓ Activated to proliferate and differentiate into effector and memory cells, secreting IL-2, a growth factor that stimulates T cell proliferation and increases the number of antigen-specific lymphocytes ↓ T cell migration to sites of infection, where they secrete cytokines ├── IFN-γ → a potent macrophage activator → macrophage activation and killing of ingested microbes └── IL-17 → recruits neutrophils and monocytes → inflammation ↓ Activated CD8+ T lymphocytes differentiate into cytotoxic T cells that kill cells harboring microbes in the cytoplasm, eliminating the reservoir of infection

B. Humoral immune response p.5

MUST KNOW The starring role

The B cell plays the starring role in humoral immunity. B cells proliferate and mature into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

MECHANISM T-dependent humoral response
B lymphocyte recognizes antigen under the influence of T helper cells ↓ Helper T cells are activated and express CD40L and secrete cytokines, which work together to stimulate the B cells ↓ Secreted cytokines from T helper cells induce immunoglobulin isotype switching and affinity maturation in the B cells ↓ Affinity maturation improves the quality of the humoral immune response ↓ Some activated B cells eventually become long-lived memory cells
COMMON CONFUSION T-dependent vs T-independent B cell responses
T-dependent
  • Protein antigens presented with helper T cell help via CD40L and cytokines
  • Gets isotype switching and affinity maturation
T-independent
  • Polysaccharides and lipids stimulate secretion mainly of IgM, because B cells can engage these antigen receptor molecules directly and initiate B cell activation
  • Called T-independent because T cells do not initiate this response

Antibody isotypes and their functions p.5

Comparison table — antibody isotype functions stated in the lecture
IsotypeFunctionExam clue
IgG and IgMActivate the complement systemComplement fixers. IgG also opsonizes, which drives type II hypersensitivity
IgAResponsible for mucosal immunityDeficiency → respiratory, GI and urogenital infections
IgEMast cell and eosinophil activation, seen in allergic reactionsThe type I hypersensitivity antibody
IgM or IgDMake up the B-cell antigen receptor complex responsible for recognizing antigenReceptor, not effector, in this role
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Cell-mediated sequence — APC presents → CD4 activated and makes IL-2 → migration → IFN-γ and IL-17 → CD8 kills infected cells.
  • Humoral needs CD40L plus cytokines from helper T cells to get isotype switching and affinity maturation.
  • Polysaccharides and lipids → mainly IgM, T-independent.
  • IgG and IgM fix complement, IgA is mucosal, IgE arms mast cells and eosinophils.

7. Hypersensitivity Reactions — overview and the ACID framework

Trans 2.01 p.5, p.9▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

Hypersensitivity implies an excessive and harmful reaction to antigen. It usually results from an imbalance between the effector mechanisms of immunity and the control mechanisms that normally limit those responses.

Exogenous environmental antigensMicrobes, dust, pollen, drugs and so on.
Endogenous antigensProduced by our own bodies. Commonly causes autoimmune diseases.
  • Development of hypersensitivity disease is often associated with the inheritance of susceptibility genes — certain types of HLA genes and non-HLA genes.
  • Classified on the basis of immune mechanism.
  • The process of tissue injury in hypersensitivity is the same as the effector mechanism of defense against infectious pathogens. The problem is that in hypersensitivity these reactions are poorly controlled, very extreme and/or misdirected.
Mnemonic (from the PDF) — ACID p.9
  • A — Atopy and Allergy → Type I
  • C — Cytotoxic, mediated by antibodies → Type II
  • I — Immune complex deposition → Type III
  • D — Delayed-type hypersensitivity → Type IV

The four types side by side Appendix, Table 6.1, p.12

Master comparison table — mechanisms of hypersensitivity reactions
TypeImmune mechanismHistopathologic lesionsPrototypical disorders
Immediate (type I)Production of IgE antibody → immediate release of vasoactive amines and other mediators from mast cells, later recruitment of inflammatory cellsVascular dilation, edema, smooth muscle contraction, mucus production, tissue injury, inflammationAnaphylaxis, allergies, bronchial asthma (atopic forms)
Antibody-mediated (type II)Production of IgG, IgM → binds antigen on target cell or tissue → phagocytosis or lysis of target cell by activated complement or Fc receptors, recruitment of leukocytesPhagocytosis and lysis of cells, inflammation, and in some diseases functional derangements without cell or tissue injuryAutoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome
Immune complex-mediated (type III)Deposition of antigen–antibody complexes → complement activation → recruitment of leukocytes by complement products and Fc receptors → release of enzymes and other toxic moleculesInflammation, necrotizing vasculitis (fibrinoid necrosis)SLE, some forms of glomerulonephritis, serum sickness, Arthus reaction
Cell-mediated (type IV)Activated T lymphocytes → (1) release of cytokines, inflammation and macrophage activation, and (2) T cell-mediated cytotoxicityPerivascular cellular infiltrates, edema, granuloma formation, cell destructionContact dermatitis, multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes, tuberculosis
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Hypersensitivity is normal defense machinery, poorly controlled, extreme or misdirected.
  • ACID — Atopy/Allergy, Cytotoxic antibody, Immune complex, Delayed.
  • Type I = IgE and mast cells. Type II = IgG/IgM against a cell or matrix. Type III = Ab–Ag complexes deposited. Type IV = T cells.
  • Susceptibility tracks with HLA and non-HLA genes.

8. Type I, Immediate Hypersensitivity

Trans 2.01 p.5–6▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

A rapid immunologic reaction occurring in a previously sensitized individual that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. These reactions are often called allergy and the antigens that elicit them are called allergens.

Cells in type I p.5

Comparison table — the three cells of type I hypersensitivity
CellLocationRoleExam clue
Mast cellNear small blood vessels, nerves, and in sub-epithelial tissuesCytoplasmic granules contain a variety of mediators. Responsible for most of the symptoms in allergic reactions because of the granules they releaseThe single most important cell of the immediate phase
BasophilPeripheral blood, in small amountsSimilar to mast cellsThe circulating counterpart of the mast cell
EosinophilTissue infiltrateDominant cell in the LATE phase of allergic reactions. Produces proteolytic enzymes that promote and prolong inflammation — major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein damage tissues, and Charcot-Leyden crystals promote inflammation and enhance TH2 responsesEosinophil = late phase, not immediate

Mediators in type I p.5

Histamine — secreted by mast cells
  • Causes intense smooth muscle contraction
  • Increases vascular permeability
  • Stimulates mucus secretion
Arachidonic acid metabolites

Leukotrienes, prostaglandin and platelet activating factor are also released in this reaction.

Proteases and enzymes

Chymase and tryptase cause tissue damage and activate the complement system through the alternative pathway because of the resultant tissue injury.

Cytokines
  • IL-4 — stimulates IgE class switching in B cells and promotes development of more Th2 cells
  • IL-5 — activates eosinophils
  • IL-13 — enhances IgE production
EXAM TRAP Which complement pathway

In type I, chymase and tryptase activate complement through the ALTERNATIVE pathway, and that happens because of the resultant tissue injury. Contrast this with type II, where IgG opsonization activates the CLASSICAL pathway.

Sequence of events p.5–6

MECHANISM Type I, from first exposure to clinical reaction
Exposure to allergen (e.g. pollen) across the mucosal lining ↓ APCs in the epithelial barriers — skin, gastric or respiratory mucosa — capture the allergen and present it to naive CD4 T cells ↓ Activation of Th2 cells — in response to the antigens and cytokines produced, the T cells differentiate into Th2 cells, which then produce several cytokines on subsequent interaction with the antigen ↓ IgE class switching in B cells → B cell production of IgE, one of the effects of Th2 activation ↓ Sensitization — once IgE is released into the blood it attaches to mast cells because they have receptors (FcεRI) for it. Complement components C5a and C3a, called anaphylatoxins, also bind receptors on mast cells and basophils ↓ Repeat exposure to allergen ↓ Activation of the mast cell and release of mediators ├── Vasoactive amines and lipid mediators → immediate hypersensitivity reaction, minutes after repeat exposure └── Cytokines → late phase reaction, 2 to 24 hours after repeat exposure

Most immediate hypersensitivity disorders are caused by a vigorous and excessive Th2 cell response, because Th2 cells stimulate IgE production and promote inflammation.

The two phases p.6

Table 2 of the PDF — comparison of immediate vs late phase p.6
FeatureImmediateLateExam clue
OnsetWithin minutes after allergen exposure, in a previously sensitized individual2 to 24 hours laterMinutes vs hours is the fastest discriminator
Main processRapid vascular reaction plus smooth muscle reactionSustained inflammation — inflammation becomes amplified and sustainedLate phase continues even without continuous allergen exposure
Important cellsMast cellsEosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes (TH2 cells)Eosinophils are the marker of lateness
Histologic findingsVasodilation, congestion and edema in a biopsyInflammatory cellular infiltrateFluid changes vs cell influx
Classic associationUrticaria / hives — an erythematous, swollen and raised skin rashAsthmaHives = immediate. Asthma = late

Who gets allergies and why p.6

  • Not all sensitized individuals develop an allergic reaction upon re-exposure.
  • Predisposition involves a multifactorial interaction between genes and environment.
  • Atopy — the tendency to develop immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Atopic individuals tend to have increased serum IgE and a strong family history of allergies or asthma. There is a familial predisposition whose exact basis is unclear, though certain inherited HLA alleles may permit reactivity to particular antigens.
  • Environmental factors — exposure to environmental pollutants is an important predisposing factor, noted in industrialized societies.
MUST KNOW Hygiene hypothesis
Early childhood exposure to certain microorganisms
  • Contributes to immune system development
  • May protect against allergic disease
Lack of exposure or being too clean
  • Impairs development of immune tolerance
  • Predisposes to allergies

Clinical presentations p.6

Systemic reaction — systemic anaphylaxis
  • Involves multiple organ systems
  • Most often follows injection of an antigen into a sensitized person, for example a bee sting
  • May also occur after ingestion, for example a food allergy
  • Can progress within minutes to shock and a potentially fatal reaction
Local reaction — depends on the portal of entry
  • Skin → localized cutaneous rash / hives
  • Nose → allergic rhinitis
  • Eyes → allergic conjunctivitis
  • Bronchi → bronchial asthma
  • GIT → diarrhea / food allergy
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Type I = antigen binds IgE on mast cells in a previously sensitized person.
  • Th2 drives the whole thing — IL-4 switches B cells to IgE and makes more Th2, IL-5 activates eosinophils, IL-13 enhances IgE.
  • Mast cell = immediate. Eosinophil = late.
  • Immediate = minutes, vasodilation-congestion-edema, urticaria. Late = 2 to 24 hours, cellular infiltrate, asthma, continues without further allergen.
  • Histamine does three things — smooth muscle contraction, vascular permeability, mucus secretion.
  • Atopy = increased serum IgE plus strong family history. Hygiene hypothesis — too clean impairs tolerance.
  • Injection (bee sting) → systemic anaphylaxis, and the local picture follows the portal of entry.

9. Type II, Antibody-Mediated Hypersensitivity

Trans 2.01 p.6–7▸
MUST KNOW Basic mechanism

Antibodies react against antigens located on cell surfaces or in the extracellular matrix (ECM). Disease then results through opsonization, phagocytosis, and antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction.

Three mechanisms of type II injury p.6–7

Comparison table — the three arms of type II hypersensitivity
ArmWhat the antibody doesResultPrototype disease
1. Opsonization and phagocytosis IgG coats / opsonizes the cell and activates the classical complement pathway. C3b and C4b are deposited on the cell. Complement activation can also produce the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC) Major mechanism responsible for the depletion of antibody-coated cells. Opsonization → the cell is recognized and destroyed. MAC creates holes in the cell membrane and kills cells by osmotic lysis. A further route is antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity (ADCC) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, transfusion reaction
2. Antibody-mediated inflammation Antibodies are deposited in the basement membrane or extracellular matrix, then activate complement, increase vascular permeability, activate leukocytes and cause cytokine release Tissue damage through inflammation. Here the antibody is not primarily destroying individual cells — the important effect is inflammation of the tissue Some forms of glomerulonephritis and vascular rejection in organ grafts
3. Antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction Antibodies target cell-surface receptors Abnormal cellular function, and it does not necessarily cause tissue injury or inflammation Myasthenia gravis (blocking) and Graves disease (stimulating)
MECHANISM Flow to easily remember type II, from the PDF p.7
1. Antibody binds cell ↓ 2. Complement activation ↓ 3. C3b / C4b opsonization ↓ 4. Phagocytosis or MAC formation or ADCC
MUST KNOW Myasthenia gravis, the worked example p.7
  • Antibody targets the acetylcholine (ACh) receptor, which is found in the motor end plate of skeletal muscle.
  • The antibody blocks the receptor, so it blocks neuromuscular transmission.
  • Main symptom is muscle weakness.

Contrast with Graves disease, where antibodies against the TSH receptor activate thyroid cells instead of blocking them.

Acute rheumatic feverStreptococcal cell wall antigen, antibody cross-reacts with myocardial antigenInflammation, macrophage activationMyocarditis, arthritis
Myasthenia gravisAcetylcholine receptorAntibody inhibits acetylcholine binding, down-modulates receptorsMuscle weakness, paralysis
Graves disease (hyperthyroidism)TSH receptorAntibody-mediated stimulation of TSH receptorsHyperthyroidism
Pernicious anemiaIntrinsic factor of gastric parietal cellsNeutralization of intrinsic factor, decreased absorption of vitamin B₁₂Abnormal erythropoiesis, anemia
EXAM TRAP Block vs stimulate

Both myasthenia gravis and Graves disease are antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction against a receptor, but the direction is opposite. ACh receptor antibody blocks → weakness. TSH receptor antibody stimulates → hyperthyroidism. Same hypersensitivity type, opposite functional effect.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Type II antibodies hit cell surfaces or ECM, not free circulating antigen.
  • IgG opsonizes → classical complement pathway → C3b and C4b → phagocytosis, or MAC with osmotic lysis, or ADCC.
  • Antibody deposited in basement membrane or ECM causes inflammation, the mechanism in glomerulonephritis and graft vascular rejection.
  • Receptor antibodies cause dysfunction without needing injury or inflammation.
  • Hapten is the keyword for drug-induced hemolysis. Maternal IgG across the placenta is the keyword for erythroblastosis fetalis.

10. Type III, Immune Complex-Mediated Hypersensitivity

Trans 2.01 p.7–8▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

Antibody (Ab) plus antigen (Ag) complexes deposited in the blood vessel wall, kidney, skin and joints produce inflammation. The antigen can be endogenous or exogenous. Immune complex-mediated diseases tend to be systemic but often preferentially involve the kidney, joints and the small blood vessels.

Pathogenesis — three phases p.7

MECHANISM The three phases in strict order
Phase 1 — immune complex formation. Protein antigen produces an immune response leading to formation of antibodies. Antibodies are secreted into the blood where they react with antigens still present in circulation and form complexes ↓ Phase 2 — immune complex deposition. Circulating antigen–antibody complexes become deposited in the blood vessels ↓ Phase 3 — immune complex-mediated inflammation and tissue injury. Once deposited in tissues, complexes initiate an acute inflammatory reaction and result in injury and damage
MUST KNOW What determines where complexes deposit p.7
  • The factors are not fully understood. The major influences seem to be the characteristics of the complexes and local vascular modifications.
  • Medium-sized Ab/Ag complexes formed under conditions of slight antigen excess are the most pathogenic.
  • Organs where blood is filtered at high pressure to form other fluids, such as urine and synovial fluid, are sites where complexes become concentrated and tend to deposit.
  • Therefore immune complex disease often affects glomeruli and joints.

Immune complex-mediated diseases p.7–8

Systemic — acute serum sickness
  • Prototype of a systemic immune complex disease
  • Was once a frequent sequela to the administration of large amounts of foreign serum during the infancy of vaccine development
  • Caused by a single exposure to a large amount of antigen, and the lesions tend to resolve because of eventual catabolism of the immune complexes
  • Historical example — serum from immunized horses used to protect against diphtheria. Vaccines are no longer prepared this way, which is why this reaction is no longer seen
Local — Arthus reaction
  • Localized area of tissue necrosis resulting from acute immune complex vasculitis
  • Often produced in the skin
  • As the antigen diffuses into the vascular wall, it binds preformed antibody and large immune complexes form locally
  • These complexes precipitate in the blood vessel walls and cause fibrinoid necrosis

Outcome — the reaction may resolve or progress to chronic disease. p.8

MUST KNOW Autoimmune diseases that use the type III mechanism p.8
  • Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
  • Polyarteritis Nodosa
  • Membranous Glomerulonephritis

Morphology — acute vasculitis p.8

  • Acute vasculitis is the principal morphologic manifestation of immune complex injury.
  • Associated with necrosis of the blood vessel and intense neutrophilic infiltration.
  • Necrotic tissue plus deposits of immune complexes, complement and plasma protein appear as a smudgy, eosinophilic area of tissue destruction — an appearance termed fibrinoid necrosis.
MUST KNOW How complexes look in the kidney p.8
Immunofluorescence microscopy

Granular, lumpy deposits of immunoglobulin and complement.

Electron microscopy

Electron-dense deposits present along the glomerular basement membrane.

Appendix master table — immune complex-mediated diseases Table 6.4, p.13

Master table — antigen involved and manifestation
DiseaseAntigen involvedClinicopathologic manifestation
Systemic lupus erythematosusNuclear antigensNephritis, skin lesions, arthritis, others
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisStreptococcal cell wall antigens, may be "planted" in glomerular basement membraneNephritis
Polyarteritis nodosaHepatitis B virus antigens in some casesSystemic vasculitis
Reactive arthritisBacterial antigens, e.g. YersiniaAcute arthritis
Serum sicknessVarious proteins, e.g. foreign serum protein (horse antithymocyte globulin)Arthritis, vasculitis, nephritis
Arthus reaction (experimental)Various foreign proteinsCutaneous vasculitis
COMMON CONFUSION Type II vs type III on immunofluorescence
Type II — antibody against a fixed tissue antigen

The antibody binds a continuous structure such as the basement membrane in Goodpasture syndrome, so staining is smooth and linear.

Type III — preformed circulating complexes land

Complexes arrive from the blood and settle in clumps, so staining is granular and lumpy. This is the pattern described for the kidney in this lecture.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Three phases — formation → deposition → inflammation and tissue injury.
  • Medium-sized complexes in slight antigen excess are most pathogenic, and they settle where blood is filtered at high pressure, so glomeruli and joints.
  • Serum sickness = systemic prototype. Arthus reaction = local, skin, fibrinoid necrosis.
  • Morphology — acute necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis and intense neutrophils.
  • Kidney — granular lumpy immunofluorescence, electron-dense deposits along the GBM.
  • Diseases named in the lecture — SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, membranous glomerulonephritis.

11. Type IV, T Cell-Mediated (Delayed-Type) Hypersensitivity

Trans 2.01 p.8–9▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

Delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) is caused by inflammation mediated primarily by CD4+ T cells and their cytokines. T-cell cytokines recruit and activate inflammatory cells, which may result in chronic and destructive inflammation.

MECHANISM Two effector routes in type IV p.8
APC presents antigen to CD4+ T cell (IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation) ├── Th1 cells → cytokines IFN-γ and TNF → macrophage activation and inflammation → inflammation dominated by activated macrophages └── Th17 cells → cytokines IL-17 and IL-22 → inflammation with a greater neutrophil component Separate route — in some diseases cytotoxic T lymphocytes directly kill tissue cells with the aid of perforins and granzymes

Both CD4+ Th1 cells and CD4+ Th17 cells contribute to this reaction.

Tuberculin reaction (PPD skin test) p.8

  • Classic example of delayed-type hypersensitivity.
  • Produced by intradermal or intracutaneous injection of purified protein derivative (PPD), a protein-containing antigen of the tubercle bacillus.
  • In a previously sensitized individual, like most Filipinos, reddening and induration of the site appear within 72 hours and thereafter slowly subside.

Morphology p.8

  • Characterized by accumulation of mononuclear cells around venules, producing perivascular "cuffing".
  • The infiltrate is mainly CD4+ T cells, shown using immunohistochemistry with anti-CD4 antibodies.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis, contact dermatitis, multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases also result from delayed type hypersensitivity reactions.
MUST KNOW Granuloma formation p.8–9
Persistent or non-degradable antigen, such as tubercle bacilli in the lungs or other tissues ↓ T cell secretes cytokines → sustained activation of macrophages ↓ Macrophages transform into epithelioid cells — large cells with abundant cytoplasm ↓ Epithelioid cells can aggregate to form multinucleated giant cells ↓ Granuloma, a small nodule, usually surrounded by lymphocytes
EXAM TRAP Th1 vs Th17 in the same reaction

Both are type IV, but the infiltrate differs. Th1-dominated inflammation = activated macrophages. Th17-triggered inflammation = greater neutrophil component. In a nickel patch-test vignette with itching, pain and neutrophil-monocyte recruitment, the cytokine is IL-17 from the Th17 subset — not IL-5, IL-10 or IL-12.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Type IV is driven primarily by CD4+ T cells and their cytokines, with CTLs killing directly via perforin and granzyme in some diseases.
  • Th1 → macrophages. Th17 → neutrophils.
  • PPD is the classic example, with reddening and induration within 72 hours in a sensitized person.
  • Morphology — perivascular cuffing by mononuclear cells, mainly CD4+.
  • Persistent antigen → epithelioid cells → multinucleated giant cells → granuloma rimmed by lymphocytes.
  • Other DTH diseases named — rheumatoid arthritis, contact dermatitis, multiple sclerosis.

12. Synchronous Session — the immune system in cancer (lung adenocarcinoma case)

Trans 2.01 p.9–10▸
The case p.9

A 62-year-old male smoker presents with persistent cough, hemoptysis and a 5-kg weight loss over two months. Chest CT shows a 4-cm mass in the right upper lobe with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A core needle biopsy confirms lung adenocarcinoma.

  • History alone suggests malignancy because of the unexplained weight loss.
  • Imaging shows a mass plus lymphadenopathy, suggesting spread.
  • Core needle biopsy is the gold standard for identifying these masses.
  • Lung cancer remains common and prevalent in our country.

Innate immunity in cancer detection p.9

  • Pattern recognition — local tissue resident macrophages and dendritic cells recognize signals from tumor cells through pattern recognition receptors.
  • Cells involved — monocytes, neutrophils, dendritic cells, innate leukocyte cells, natural killer (NK) cells.
  • Transformed malignant cells express DAMPs. When a cell becomes neoplastic it undergoes biochemical, structural and metabolic changes, and once normal cells transform into malignant cells they express DAMP. This is the key protein or structural change that lets innate immune cells recognize the tumor as foreign.
  • NOD-like receptors and the inflammasome, cytokines and mediators — innate receptors (toll-like, nod-like, inflammasomes) are found in the cytosol of all cells, and cytokines and mediators are released during cell damage.
  • Result — they phagocytose tumor debris and secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-12, TNF-α) to recruit innate immunity cells to remove the tumor cells, done by macrophages and neutrophils.
MUST KNOW Remember box from the PDF

NO SENSITIZATION, NO IMMEDIATE RESPONSE, NO MEMORY. This is because innate immunity relies solely on pattern recognition. It is a very simple type of immunity already present in our body, and it can detect cancer cells.

Adaptive immunity in cancer p.9

MECHANISM The two arms against a tumor
MHC II → CD4 → cytokines → T-helper cells which then kill microbes by inflammation, secreting interferon gamma and interleukin 2, which trigger: · Dendritic cells to activate macrophages · Upregulation of MHC expression · Sustained response to effectively kill tumor cells ↓ MHC I → CD8 → cytotoxic T lymphocytes, the main effectors. They recognize the tumor antigen on MHC I, which is presented on all nucleated cells, so they can survey tumor cells directly ↓ Killing — perforin from cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes bores holes in the cytoplasm of tumor cells, which then secrete granzymes that activate caspases and initiate apoptosis
Antigen capture and presentation
  • Tumor cells express tumor antigens such as viral oncogenes or mutated oncoproteins, for example mutant KRAS / EGFR in lung adenocarcinoma.
  • Dying tumor cells are ingested by dendritic cells, which migrate to draining mediastinal lymph nodes.
  • Dendritic cells present antigens to CD4 T cells, recruiting helper and regulatory T cells to destroy cancer cells through inflammation.
  • Dendritic cells cross-present tumor peptides on MHC class I to CD8 T cells.
  • Tumor cells are ingested by APCs, particularly dendritic cells and activated macrophages.
MUST KNOW Adaptive immunity needs two signals p.9
  • Signal 1 — TCR recognizes the peptide on the MHC complex.
  • Signal 2 — co-stimulation of B7 on the dendritic cell binding CD28 on the T cell.
  • Signal 1 without signal 2 produces anergy, which is the basis of tumor tolerance.
Humoral arm against tumors
  • When the Fas ligand on cytotoxic T lymphocytes binds the Fas receptor on the tumor cell, this triggers the extrinsic apoptotic pathway.
  • Some antibodies may be generated against tumor cells, coating the tumor cells and triggering opsonization.
  • In humoral immunity it is the B cells that secrete antibodies, after maturing into plasma cells.
  • Also antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
  • Mostly seen in breast cancers and lymphoma, not so much in lung carcinoma.

How tumor cells evade the immune system p.9–10

MUST KNOW Immune checkpoints
  • Activation of immune checkpoints is one of the most clinically important mechanisms of immune evasion.
  • Immune checkpoint — the built-in brakes for our immune system. They are naturally occurring and are needed so that lymphocytes do not react to everything inside the body, giving them the chance to recognize self-antigens so there is no immune reaction against our own body.
  • The lecture's analogy — T lymphocytes are security guards doing surveillance. A normal healthy cell has a receptor, like an ID badge, telling the T cell it is a normal own cell that should not be harmed. This induces peripheral tolerance.
Forms of peripheral tolerance exploited by tumors p.10
AnergyInstead of two signals there is only one — the antigen is presented but the co-stimulatory signal does not happen, so the T cells do not react and let normal cells pass by.
Suppression of regulatory T cellsReceptors for regulatory T cells are downregulated, so T cells will not react to normal cells.
Deletion by apoptosisYour own T cells recognize your own body, as opposed to central tolerance.

Upregulation of PD-L1 on tumor cells → binds PD-1 on T lymphocytes.

Summary of the immune system in lung cancer p.10

Comparison table — innate vs adaptive vs evasion vs therapy in the cancer case
StageKey points from the lectureExam clue
Innate immunity — first responseNo prior sensitization required. Very fast but the reaction is very basic or small. Only relies on pattern recognition. Effector cells — NK cells detect and kill "missing-self" tumor cells lacking MHC I, and dendritic cells and macrophages capture and present tumor antigens"Missing self" = no MHC I = NK cell target
Adaptive immunity — antigen-specific killingDendritic cells prime CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes and CD4+ Th1 cells, which provide cytokine help through IFN-γ and IL-2, recruiting other inflammatory cells in the backgroundDC is the primer for both CD4 and CD8
Immune evasion by the tumorPD-L1 upregulation, MHC I loss, Tregs/MDSCs and TGF-β create an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Immune tolerance through CTLA-4 and PD-L1 is one of the most important mechanisms by which tumors evade our immune systemMHC I loss escapes CD8 but invites NK killing
Checkpoint blockade restores immunityUsed to cure cancers with promising results. Patients with adenocarcinoma once had less than a year to live and now can live 3 or more years with targeted therapy. Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1/PD-L1, releasing the brakes on exhausted CD8+ T cells. Activated T cells then recognize tumor neoantigens presented on MHC class I, leading to targeted cell lysis via perforin and granzyme releasePembrolizumab = PD-1 on T cell binding PD-L1 on tumor cell
Cost — immune-related adverse eventsThe immune system is not perfect, so checks and balances are needed. Stopping the brakes may cause loss of peripheral tolerance and induce inflammation in other parts of the body. Loss of peripheral tolerance causes colitis, thyroiditis and pneumonitis, managed with corticosteroidsCheckpoint colitis is a type IV reaction
Continuation of the case p.10

Over the course of targeted chemotherapy (checkpoint inhibitor therapy), the patient developed severe colitis — severe diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever and hematochezia.

EXAM TRAP Three traps from the lecture's own answer key p.10
  • The innate cell that recognizes abnormal stress ligands on tumor cells and gives direct cellular cytotoxicity without prior sensitization is the NK cell. Naive CD8+ lymphocytes, B lymphocytes and plasma cells are all part of adaptive immunity.
  • Pembrolizumab targets PD-1 on T cells binding PD-L1 on tumor cells, not CD28–B7 and not Fas–Fas ligand.
  • Checkpoint-inhibitor colitis is type IV, T cell-mediated. It is not type I, because there is no mast cell degranulation in severe colitis.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Innate anti-tumor immunity — no sensitization, no immediate response, no memory, only pattern recognition of DAMPs, with NK cells killing MHC I-negative "missing self" cells.
  • Adaptive — MHC II/CD4 helps, MHC I/CD8 kills via perforin then granzymes then caspases.
  • Signal 1 without signal 2 = anergy = the basis of tumor tolerance.
  • Evasion — PD-L1 up, MHC I lost, Tregs and TGF-β. CTLA-4 and PD-L1 are the key tolerance checkpoints.
  • Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1/PD-L1 and its cost is immune-related colitis, thyroiditis and pneumonitis, treated with corticosteroids.

Part 2 — Diseases of Immunity 2 (Trans 2.02)

Tolerance → causes of autoimmunity → autoimmune diseases → immunodeficiencies → HIV/AIDS → transplant rejection → amyloidosis

13. Immunologic Tolerance — central and peripheral

Trans 2.02 p.1–2▸
MUST KNOW Core definitions
Immunologic tolerance
Lack of response from our body when it is presented with or exposed to a lymphocyte.
Self tolerance
The ability of our body to recognize our own cell and choose not to react with it. This principle underlies the ability to live in harmony with our own cells and tissues.
Self-antigens
Generated by cells through normal cell metabolism or because of viral or intracellular bacterial infection.

Mechanisms divide into two groups depending on the site of immunoregulation — central tolerance and peripheral tolerance.

A. Central tolerance p.1

Occurs in the thymus (T cells) or bone marrow (B cells). Two mechanisms.

1. Negative selection (clonal deletion) — T cells
  • Occurs when immature T cells express TCRs specific for self-antigens and encounter these antigens in the thymus
  • Signals are produced that result in killing of the cells by apoptosis
  • Begins with antigen presentation of self-antigens to naive T cells in the thymus
  • When the T cell has a receptor that can identify the self antigen, it undergoes clonal deletion
  • Autoimmune Regulator (AIRE) — stimulates the expression of peripheral tissue-restricted self-antigens in the thymus and is critical for the deletion of immature T cells specific for these antigens
  • Some cells that do not recognize the self-antigens in the thymus develop into regulatory T cells
2. Receptor editing (and deletion) — B cells
  • When developing B cells recognize self-antigens in the bone marrow, they undergo antigen-receptor gene management to express new antigen receptors not specific for self-antigens
  • Antigen receptor gene rearrangement is repeated so new non-self-reactive receptors are made
  • If receptor editing does not occur, the cells undergo apoptosis, thereby removing the dangerous lymphocytes from the mature pool
EXAM TRAP Central tolerance is not foolproof

Not all self-antigens may be present in the thymus and bone marrow, so some lymphocytes bearing receptors for such auto-antigens escape into the periphery. This is exactly why a second mechanism (peripheral tolerance) exists to detect self-reactive lymphocytes that escaped negative selection.

B. Peripheral tolerance p.1–2

Occurs in other organs, tissues or in the bloodstream. Three mechanisms.

1. Anergy
  • T cells are rendered unresponsive
  • Activation of an antigen-specific T cell requires two signals — recognition of antigen in association with MHC on the APC surface, plus a set of second signals from APCs
  • If antigen is presented without adequate levels of co-stimulators, cells become anergic
  • Because costimulator molecules are not expressed or are weakly expressed on resting APCs, an encounter between auto-reactive T cells and their self-antigens on these APCs leads to anergy
  • T cells recognizing self-antigens also receive an inhibitory signal from receptors structurally homologous to CD28 — the immune checkpoint inhibitors PD-1 and CTLA-4, the "brakes" of the immune system, expressed on a wide variety of cells
  • Anergy also affects mature B cells in peripheral tissues, especially in the absence of specific helper T cells, so they cannot respond to later antigenic stimulation and may die
2. Suppression by regulatory T cells
  • Suppression by regulatory T cells is used against self-antigens, and also against the fetus and commensal microbes
  • Tregs suppress immune responses by inhibitory activity through the secretion of IL-10 and TGF-β
  • These inhibit lymphocyte activation and effector functions
3. Deletion by apoptosis
  • Occurs in the peripheral tissues when T cells that recognize self-antigens receive signals promoting death by apoptosis
  • T cells that recognize self-antigens may also recognize apoptotic signals and undergo deletion
MUST KNOW Why tumors and viruses care about this p.2

Some tumors and viruses use the same pathways of immune regulation to escape immune attack. This has led to the development of antibodies that block CTLA-4, PD-1 and its ligand PD-L1 for tumor immunotherapy, for example in lung cancer. By removing the brakes of the immune response, these antibodies act against tumors. This is the same mechanism as Pembrolizumab from Part 1.

COMMON CONFUSION Central vs peripheral tolerance
FeatureCentral tolerancePeripheral toleranceFast distinction
SiteThymus (T cells), bone marrow (B cells)Other organs, tissues, bloodstreamGenerative organ vs everywhere else
MechanismsNegative selection / clonal deletion, receptor editingAnergy, suppression by Tregs, deletion by apoptosisTwo mechanisms vs three
Key moleculeAIRE in the thymusPD-1 and CTLA-4AIRE puts tissue antigens in the thymus, checkpoints brake mature T cells
PurposeDelete self-reactive lymphocytes before they leaveCatch the ones that escapedPeripheral is the backup system
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Central = thymus and bone marrow. T cells → negative selection / clonal deletion by apoptosis, helped by AIRE. B cells → receptor editing, or apoptosis if editing fails.
  • Cells that do not recognize self-antigens in the thymus can become regulatory T cells.
  • Peripheral = anergy, Treg suppression (IL-10 and TGF-β), deletion by apoptosis.
  • Anergy = signal 1 without signal 2, reinforced by PD-1 and CTLA-4, the brakes.
  • Central tolerance is not foolproof, which is why peripheral tolerance exists.

14. Causes of Autoimmunity

Trans 2.02 p.2▸
MUST KNOW Core idea

Causes of autoimmunity are multifactorial. It arises from a combination of (1) the inheritance of susceptibility genes that contribute to the breakdown of self-tolerance and (2) environmental triggers, such as infections and tissue damage, that promote the stimulation of self-reactive lymphocytes.

A. Gene susceptibility p.2

  • Having certain HLA genes is among the risks known to be strongly associated with the development of autoimmunity.
  • Multiple non-MHC genes are also associated with various autoimmune diseases. It is hypothesized that their products affect general mechanisms of immune regulation and self tolerance.
MUST KNOW Ankylosing spondylitis and HLA-B27
  • Persons who inherit this Class I HLA allele have a 100 to 200-fold greater chance of developing the disease compared with those who do not carry the allele.
  • Despite the strong association, the presence of the HLA gene itself is not the cause of the disease.

B. Other causes of autoimmunity p.2

Autoimmune reactions may also be triggered by infections. The two mechanisms that link infections and autoimmunity are induction of costimulators on APCs and molecular mimicry.

1. Induction of costimulators on APCs

Infections may upregulate the expression of costimulators on APCs. If those cells are presenting self-antigens, the result may be a breakdown of anergy and activation of T cells specific for the self-antigens.

2. Molecular mimicry
  • Some microbes express antigens that share similar amino acid sequences with self-antigens
  • The immune response against a microbial antigen may then activate self-reactive lymphocytes
  • Classic example — rheumatic heart disease, where antibodies against streptococcal proteins cross-react with myocardial proteins, causing heart inflammation
Other infection-related routes named in the lecture
  • Some viruses, such as EBV and HIV, can cause polyclonal B cell activation that may result in production of autoantibodies.
  • Tissue injury common in infections may release and structurally modify self-antigens, creating new antigens able to activate T cells.
  • Infections may induce cytokines that recruit lymphocytes, including potentially self-reacting lymphocytes, to the site of self-antigens.
3. Environment

Display of tissue antigen may be altered by environmental insults. Ultraviolet radiation causes cell death and may lead to exposure of nuclear antigens, which elicit pathological immune responses in lupus.

4. Gender bias

Autoimmune diseases are more common in women than men. The underlying mechanisms are not understood but may involve the effects of hormones and possibly some unknown genes on the X chromosome.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Autoimmunity = susceptibility genes plus an environmental trigger.
  • HLA-B27 and ankylosing spondylitis — 100 to 200-fold risk, but the gene is not the cause.
  • Infection links autoimmunity by inducing costimulators (breaks anergy) and molecular mimicry.
  • Molecular mimicry prototype = rheumatic heart disease, streptococcal antibody cross-reacting with myocardium.
  • EBV and HIV → polyclonal B cell activation. UV light → exposes nuclear antigens in lupus.
  • Women are affected more than men, mechanism unknown.

15. Autoimmune Diseases — general features

Trans 2.02 p.2▸
MUST KNOW General features of autoimmune diseases
  • Tends to be chronic, sometimes with relapses and remissions, and the damage is often progressive.
  • There is currently no cure for autoimmune diseases. Management relies on controlling the inflammation that is inappropriately directed against our own body.
  • Clinical and pathologic manifestations are determined by the nature of the underlying immune response — T-cell mediated inflammation or Ab–Ag complex formation and deposition of hypersensitivity reactions result in autoimmune diseases.
  • This also explains why clinical and serological presentations are similar for most autoimmune diseases.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Chronic, relapsing-remitting, progressive, no cure — treatment controls inflammation only.
  • The presentation is decided by which hypersensitivity mechanism is doing the damage, which is why these diseases look alike.

16. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

Trans 2.02 p.3–6▸
MUST KNOW Core idea and hallmark

SLE is the most well known and studied autoimmune disease, called in lecture the poster child for autoimmune diseases. Its hallmark is the production of antinuclear antibodies (ANAs). Injury is caused by deposition of immune complexes and binding of antibodies to various tissues — that is, a type III mechanism with some type II.

Table 3 of the PDF — SLE at a glance p.3
AutoantibodiesMultiple organ systemWho is affected
Antinuclear antibodies against DNA, histones, non-histone RNA, and nucleolus

Anti-dsDNA, Anti-Sm

Immune complex deposition		 Acute, insidious

Chronic, remitting and relapsing, often febrile illness

Skin, joints, kidney and serosal membranes		 Women, 17 to 55 years old

2 to 3 fold higher in Blacks and Hispanics
MUST KNOW The two virtually diagnostic antibodies
  • Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Sm (Smith) antigen are virtually diagnostic of the disease.
  • Their presence and levels in the blood help in diagnosing and managing patients.
  • These and other autoantibodies are pathogenic either by forming immune complexes or by attacking their target cells.
Presentation and epidemiology p.3
  • Presentation may be acute or insidious, and may be chronic, remitting and relapsing, often febrile.
  • Injury to the skin, joints, kidney and serosal membrane is most obvious, but any organ may be affected.
  • Affects mostly women aged 17 to 55 years old, most commonly in the 20s to 30s, and is mostly seen in Blacks and Hispanics versus Whites.
SLICC criteria p.3

The Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) criteria were established by the American College of Rheumatology and revised by SLICC in 2012. A patient is said to have SLE if 4 of the clinical and immunologic criteria are present, including at least one clinical and one immunologic criterion.

Spectrum of antibodies in SLE — ANA fluorescence patterns p.3

  • Indirect immunofluorescence for ANA is the most widely used method to detect the presence of antinuclear antibodies.
  • The pattern of fluorescence determines the type of antibody present in patient serum.
  • Patterns are sensitive but not absolutely specific — many autoantibodies may be present and combinations of patterns are frequently seen. Still, the staining pattern has diagnostic value and remains one of the cornerstones in diagnosing autoimmune diseases.
Table 4 of the PDF — patterns of fluorescence p.3
PatternDescriptionAntibodies forDisease
HomogeneousDiffuse nuclear staining with a prominent rim or peripheral staining patterndsDNA, nuclear envelope proteinsSLE
SpeckledPresence of uniform or variable sized speckles. Frequently observed, making it the least specific patternNon-DNA constituents — e.g. Sm antigen, ribonucleoprotein, SS-A and SS-B reactive antigensSjögren syndrome
NucleolarPresence of discrete spots of fluorescence within the nucleusRNASystemic sclerosis
CentromericStaining of centromeresCentromeresSystemic sclerosis
EXAM TRAP Pattern to disease pairing

Speckled is the least specific pattern because it is the most frequently observed — do not use it to clinch a diagnosis. In this table, homogeneous → SLE, speckled → Sjögren, and both nucleolar AND centromeric → systemic sclerosis.

Other antibodies in SLE — antiphospholipid antibodies p.3

  • Aside from ANAs, SLE patients have a host of other autoantibodies — some are directed against red cells, platelets and lymphocytes, and others react with phospholipid-binding proteins.
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies (APAS) are present in about 40% of SLE patients and are specific for epitopes of plasma proteins that are revealed when the proteins are in complex with phospholipids.
  • They react against RBCs and platelets and interfere with in vitro clotting tests like PTT (partial thromboplastin time), and cross-react with syphilis serology.
  • They are therefore sometimes called "lupus anticoagulants", which is actually a misnomer.
MUST KNOW Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APAS)
  • Despite the observed clotting delays in vitro, patients with APAS have complications related to excessive clotting, placing them in a hypercoagulable state.
  • Patients may develop venous and arterial thrombosis, associated with recurrent spontaneous miscarriages and focal cerebral or ocular ischemia.
Primary APAS

The patient develops APAS and the clinical syndrome without associated SLE. Idiopathic — signs and symptoms of a hypercoagulable state without SLE or other autoimmune disorders.

Secondary APAS

The patient has symptoms in association with SLE. Acquired due to the presence of an underlying disease.

EXAM TRAP The reversed cause-and-effect of lupus anticoagulant

The name says anticoagulant and the in vitro PTT is prolonged, but the in vivo problem is thrombosis. The lecture explicitly calls the name a misnomer. Also remember it can produce a false positive syphilis serology.

Lupus erythematosus (LE) cells p.3

  • Seen when blood is agitated in vitro or mixed vigorously in a test tube — if cell nuclei are exposed, the antinuclear antibodies can bind to them.
  • In vivo, nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern and become homogeneous, producing "LE bodies" or "hematoxylin bodies".
  • LE cells are phagocytic leukocytes that have engulfed the denatured nucleus of an injured cell.
  • Demonstration of LE cells in vitro was used in the past to test for SLE, but with better ANA detection techniques this test is now largely of historical interest.

Etiology and pathogenesis p.3–4

MECHANISM The fundamental defect

The fundamental defect in SLE is a failure of the mechanisms that maintain self-tolerance.

Genetic+ Immunologic+ Environmental= Failure of self tolerance

What produces these failures of self tolerance remains unidentified, but both genetic and environmental factors play a role.

Genetic
  • Plays a big role in disease development
  • 20% of clinically unaffected first-degree relatives have autoantibodies and other clinically detectable immune abnormalities
  • HLA-DQ — specific alleles of the HLA-DQ locus are linked to production of anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm and antiphospholipid antibodies, although the relative risk is small
  • Inherent deficiencies in complement proteins C1q, C2 or C4 may impair removal of circulating immune complexes, favoring tissue deposition
  • Genetic predisposition alone is not enough — a faulty immune system must also play a role
Immunologic
  • Failure of self tolerance — self-reactive B or T cells remain in circulation instead of being destroyed or modified
  • Self-nucleic acids may mimic their microbial counterparts by producing type I interferons via activation of toll-like receptors in the cell, which may stimulate reproduction of pathogenic autoantibodies and induce inflammation
  • Increased cytokine production
Environmental
  • Exposure to UV light can exacerbate disease. UV irradiation may induce apoptosis in cells or alter DNA so that recognition by TLRs is enhanced, and UV light may stimulate keratinocytes to produce IL-1, a cytokine that promotes inflammation
  • Drugs — hydralazine, procainamide and D-penicillamine can induce an SLE-like response in humans
  • Gender bias

Clinical manifestations — skin p.4

Gross
  • Butterfly / malar rash — characteristic erythema along the bridge of the nose and cheeks, seen in half of patients. A similar rash may appear on extremities and trunk
  • Discoid rash — discoid-shaped rash or a more diffuse presentation
  • Skin lesions show varying degrees of edema, erythema, scaliness, follicular plugging and skin atrophy, surrounded by an elevated erythematous border
Microscopy
  • Immune complex deposition
  • Vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer of the epidermis
  • Variable edema at the dermo-epidermal junction and perivascular inflammation in the dermis
  • Prominent vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis
  • Immunofluorescence microscopy shows deposition of immunoglobulin and complement along the dermoepidermal junction

Clinical manifestations — kidney and the six classes of lupus nephritis p.4–5

  • Clinically significant glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis are also common.
  • Glomerular lesions are the result of deposition of immune complexes on the glomerular basement membrane, in the mesangium, and sometimes throughout the glomerulus — this is the type III hypersensitivity mechanism.
  • There are six patterns of glomerular disease in SLE, which sometimes overlap, and over time lesions may evolve from one class to another.
Master table — the six classes of lupus nephritis (LN)
ClassNameDefining featuresKey recall point
IMinimal mesangial LNVery uncommon. No light microscopic changes. Immune complex deposition in the mesangium identified only by immunofluorescence and electron microscopyNormal on H&E — you need IF or EM
IIMesangial proliferative LNMesangial cell proliferation with accumulation of mesangial matrix, and granular mesangial deposits of immunoglobulin and complement. Without involvement of glomerular capillariesMesangium only, capillaries spared
IIIFocal LNInvolvement of less than 50% of glomeruli. Lesions may be segmental (only a portion) or global (entire glomerulus). Affected glomeruli may show swelling and proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, WBC accumulation, capillary necrosis and hyaline thrombiLess than 50% is the whole definition
IVDiffuse LNMost common and most severe pattern. Lesions identical to class III but half or more of the glomeruli are affected, segmental or global. Proliferation comes from endothelial, mesangial and epithelial cells, the epithelial cells producing cellular crescents that fill Bowman's space. Subendothelial immune complex deposits cause circumferential thickening of the capillary wall forming wire-loop structures on light microscopy. Complexes are readily detected by EM and immunofluorescenceWire-loop = class IV, and ≥50% of glomeruli
VMembranous LNDiffuse thickening of capillary walls due to subepithelial immune complexes, similar to idiopathic membranous nephropathy. Complexes are accompanied by increased basement membrane-like material, producing "spikes" between deposits visible by silver stain. Usually accompanied by severe proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome, and may occur concurrently with focal or diffuse LNSubepithelial deposits plus silver-stain spikes plus nephrotic syndrome
VIAdvanced sclerosing LNSclerosis of more than 90% of the glomeruli and represents end-stage renal diseaseOver 90% sclerosed = end stage
EXAM TRAP Deposit location decides the class
Mesangial depositsClass I (IF/EM only) and class II (with mesangial proliferation).
Subendothelial depositsClass IV → wire-loop thickening of the capillary wall.
Subepithelial depositsClass V → membranous, silver-stain spikes, nephrotic syndrome.

Class III and class IV differ only by extent — under 50% versus 50% or more of glomeruli. The lesions themselves are identical.

Clinical manifestations — cardiac p.5

Diffuse leaflet thickening
May be associated with stenosis or regurgitation.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis
AKA vulvar endocarditis
Nonbacterial verrucous or warty endocarditis taking the form of single or multiple 1 to 3 mm warty deposits on ANY surface of the leaflet of any heart valve. Used to be common before the widespread use of steroids.
Pericarditis
Inflammation of the pericardial membrane. Later the membranes may become thickened, opaque and covered with shaggy fibrous tissue, leading to partial or total obliteration of the pericardial cavity.

Variants of SLE p.5–6

These variants are unique because cutaneous involvement is the exclusive or most prominent feature.

Comparison table — the three SLE variants
VariantSkin pictureSystemic involvementAntibody / HLA association
Chronic discoid lupus erythematosusPredominant skin manifestations in the face and scalp (discoid lesions). Plaques show varying edema, erythema, scaliness, follicular plugging and skin atrophy surrounded by an elevated erythematous borderSystemic involvement is rare — disease remains confined to the skin, though a small percentage may develop multi-system manifestations after many yearsAntibodies to double stranded DNA are rarely present
Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosusWidespread skin lesions, non-scarringMost patients have mild systemic symptoms consistent with SLE. Appears to have features intermediate between chronic discoid LE and SLEStrong association with antibodies to SS-A antigen and with the HLA-DR3 genotype
Drug induced lupus erythematosusSLE-like syndrome developing in patients receiving drugs — hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, D-penicillamineSLE-like syndromeAntibodies specific for histone, associated with the HLA-DR4 allele, are frequently seen
EXAM TRAP Similar names, different antibodies
  • Subacute cutaneous LE → SS-A antibodies and HLA-DR3.
  • Drug induced LE → anti-histone antibodies and HLA-DR4.
  • Chronic discoid LE → anti-dsDNA is rarely present.
  • From the Part 1 formative quiz answer key — drug induced SLE is not the pair for anti-DNA and anti-Sm, because those two belong to classic SLE.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Hallmark = ANAs. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are virtually diagnostic. Mechanism = immune complex deposition.
  • Women 17 to 55, peaking in the 20s to 30s, 2 to 3 fold higher in Blacks and Hispanics.
  • SLICC — 4 criteria, with at least one clinical and one immunologic.
  • ANA patterns — homogeneous → SLE, speckled → Sjögren (least specific), nucleolar and centromeric → systemic sclerosis.
  • APAS in about 40% — prolonged PTT in vitro but hypercoagulable in vivo, with thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage and cerebral or ocular ischemia.
  • LE cell = a phagocyte that has swallowed a denatured nucleus.
  • Complement deficiency (C1q, C2, C4) impairs clearance of immune complexes. UV light exposes nuclear antigens and stimulates keratinocyte IL-1.
  • Skin — malar rash in half of patients, microscopy shows vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer with IgG along the dermoepidermal junction.
  • Kidney — class IV is most common and severe, with wire-loops. Class V is membranous with nephrotic syndrome. Class VI is over 90% sclerosis, end stage.
  • Heart — Libman-Sacks, 1 to 3 mm warty deposits on any surface of any valve.

17. Rheumatoid Arthritis and Sjögren Syndrome

Trans 2.02 p.6▸

B. Rheumatoid arthritis p.6

MUST KNOW Core idea

RA is a chronic inflammatory disease triggered by autoantibodies specific for citrullinated peptides (CCPs), peptides in which arginine residues are converted to citrulline.

Anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs)
Diagnostic markers frequently detected in the serum of patients.
Rheumatoid factor (RF)
IgM and IgA autoantibodies that bind to the Fc regions of IgG, that is, RF is directed against the Fc portion of IgG.
Target tissues
Joints and blood vessels.
Hypersensitivity link
Listed in Part 1 among the diseases resulting from delayed type (type IV) hypersensitivity reactions. Trans 2.01 p.8

The lecture covers RA briefly in text and leans on the figure for the clinical and histologic picture.

EXAM TRAP What RF actually targets

Rheumatoid factor is an IgM and IgA antibody directed AGAINST the Fc portion of IgG. It is an antibody against another antibody. Do not confuse it with ACPAs, which target citrullinated peptides and are the diagnostic marker emphasized here.

C. Sjögren syndrome p.6

MUST KNOW Core definition

A chronic disease characterized by dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) resulting from an immunologically-mediated disruption of the lacrimal and salivary glands, specifically their destruction through lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis.

Clinical manifestations
  • Blurring of vision, burning and itching sensation around the eyes, with thick secretions around the conjunctival area due to the dry eyes.
  • Difficulty swallowing solid food and decreased ability to taste, due to decreased saliva, with cracks and fissures around the mouth and dryness of the buccal mucosa.
  • Parotid gland enlargement is present in half of the patients.
  • Extraglandular disease is seen in few women — bronchitis, pneumonitis, synovitis, peripheral neuropathy.
  • The typical patient — female, complaining of dry eyes and dry mouth, with a possibly enlarged parotid gland.
Pathogenesis
  • Pathogenesis remains obscure like most autoimmune diseases, but aberrant T-cell and B-cell activation are always implicated.
  • The initiating cause may be a viral infection of the salivary glands, causing local cell death and release of tissue self-antigens.
  • Antibodies directed against two ribonucleoprotein antigens — SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La) — can be detected in as many as 90% of patients and are considered the serologic markers of the disease. Rheumatoid factor is also present.
  • Weak associations with certain HLA alleles — HLA-B8, HLA-DR3, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1.
  • Marginal zone lymphoma — about 5% of Sjögren patients develop this lymphoma, with an incidence that is 40-fold greater compared with normal individuals.
MUST KNOW The lip / salivary gland biopsy

If a biopsy is done on the lip or salivary gland, you see intense lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration with ductal epithelial hyperplasia. The lecture's point — the duct is obstructed, which is why there is dry mouth, since there is no lumen in the duct for saliva to pass through.

This is the correct answer in the Part 1 formative quiz for a woman with burning eyes, blurred vision, dry eyes and dry buccal mucosa — the lip biopsy shows marked lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrates in the minor salivary glands. Trans 2.01 p.11

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • RA — autoantibodies against citrullinated peptides. ACPAs are the diagnostic markers. RF targets the Fc portion of IgG and is IgM and IgA.
  • Sjögren — dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) plus dry mouth (xerostomia) from destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands.
  • SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La) in up to 90% of patients are the serologic markers. Speckled ANA pattern.
  • Parotid enlargement in half. Biopsy = lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration with ductal epithelial hyperplasia.
  • 5% develop marginal zone lymphoma, a 40-fold increased incidence.

18. Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma) and other less common autoimmune diseases

Trans 2.02 p.6–7▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

Characterized by chronic inflammation from autoimmunity leading to widespread damage of small blood vessels and progressive fibrosis of the skin, GI tract, kidney, heart, lungs and small blood vessels. It predominantly affects women, 50 to 60 years old, and is more severe in African-Americans.

Two major categories p.6

Diffuse systemic sclerosis
  • Widespread skin involvement
  • Rapid progression
  • Early visceral involvement
Limited systemic sclerosis
  • Skin involvement often confined to the fingers, forearms and the face
  • Visceral involvement occurs late, so the clinical course is relatively benign
  • Some patients may develop CREST syndrome
Mnemonic (from the PDF) — CREST syndrome
  • C — Calcinosis
  • R — Raynaud's phenomenon
  • E — Esophageal dysmotility
  • S — Sclerodactyly
  • T — Telangiectasia

The two antinuclear antibodies p.6

There are two ANAs strongly associated with systemic sclerosis and highly specific for it.

Comparison table — the two systemic sclerosis antibodies
AntibodyDirected againstClinical correlationExam clue
Anti-Scl 70DNA topoisomerase IPatients are more likely to have pulmonary fibrosis and peripheral vascular diseasesScl-70 → the diffuse, organ-damaging end. Nucleolar ANA pattern
Anti-centromereCentromeresFound in 20 to 30% of patients, who tend to have CREST syndrome or the limited presentationCentromere → CREST / limited. Centromeric ANA pattern
EXAM TRAP Do not swap the two scleroderma antibodies

Anti-Scl 70 pairs with systemic sclerosis (the diffuse, fibrosing form), not with CREST. Anti-centromere pairs with CREST / limited disease. The Part 1 formative quiz explicitly lists "CREST, Scl-70" as an INCORRECT pairing. In the same question Sjögren with anti-centromere is also wrong, and the correct pair given is inflammatory myopathy with Jo-1, which targets histidyl-tRNA synthetase and is strongly associated with polymyositis / dermatomyositis and antisynthetase syndrome. Trans 2.01 p.10–11

Pathogenesis p.6–7

MECHANISM The equation and the three interrelated processes
T & B cell activation+ Vascular damage+ Collagen deposition= Systemic sclerosis

The cause has still not been identified, but the disease likely results from three interrelated processes — autoimmunity, vascular damage and fibrosis.

A. Autoimmunity

CD4 T cells respond to an unidentified antigen that accumulates in the skin and induce cytokine release that activates inflammatory cells and fibrosis or fibroblast proliferation.

B. Vascular damage (microvascular disease)
  • CD4+ T cell is consistently present early in the course and may be the initial lesion
  • Intimal proliferation of the lumen is evident in the digital arteries
  • Capillary dilatation and destruction are also common
  • The cause of vascular injury is still unknown — it could be the initiating event or the result of chronic inflammation
  • Over time, widespread narrowing of the microvasculature leads to ischemic injury and scarring
C. Fibrosis SHOULD KNOW
  • May be the culmination of accumulation of alternatively activated macrophages, fibrogenic cytokines produced by infiltrating leukocytes, hyperresponsiveness of fibroblasts to these cytokines, and scarring following ischemic damage
  • There is some evidence that fibroblasts from patients have an intrinsic abnormality causing excessive collagen production, based on cultured fibroblasts, though whether or how this relates to pathogenesis in vivo is unknown

Gross and histologic features p.7

Gross
  • Blank, mask-like face
  • Skin appears shiny, very smooth and drawn tight, with the lips often pressed tightly together
  • Hands may show claw deformity with ulcerated fingertips
  • These findings are due to skin fibrosis and ischemia from the vascular injury that produces the digital ulcers
Histologic
  • Skin biopsy shows extensive deposition of dense collagen in the dermis
  • Virtual absence of hair follicles and sweat glands, with foci of inflammation
  • The absence of hair follicles and sweat glands is what makes the skin shiny and smooth

Systemic manifestations of systemic sclerosis p.7 SHOULD KNOW

  • Raynaud phenomenon — numbness and tingling of the fingers and toes caused by episodic vasoconstriction of arteries and arterioles.
  • Dysphagia from esophageal fibrosis and resultant hypomotility, present in more than 50% of patients. Destruction of the esophageal wall leads to atony and dilation, especially at its lower end.
  • Abdominal pain, intestinal obstruction, or malabsorption syndrome with weight loss and anemia from small intestine involvement.
  • Respiratory difficulties from pulmonary fibrosis may result in right-sided cardiac dysfunction. Myocardial fibrosis may cause arrhythmias or cardiac failure.
