  • Proteinuria occurs in as many as 30% of patients, but is rarely severe enough to cause nephrotic syndrome.
  • The most ominous manifestation is malignant hypertension, with subsequent development of renal failure. In its absence, disease progression may be slow.

E. Other less common autoimmune diseases p.7

Comparison table — mixed connective tissue disease vs IgG4-related disease
FeatureMixed connective tissue diseaseIgG4-related disease
Defining conceptClinical features that overlap with SLE, scleroderma and polymyositisA constellation of disorders characterized by IgG4 antibody-producing plasma cells, T cells, fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis and increased serum IgG4
Clinical pictureSynovitis of fingers, Raynaud phenomenon and mild myositis, with modest renal involvementIncludes Mikulicz syndrome, Riedel thyroiditis, idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis, autoimmune pancreatitis, and inflammatory pseudotumors of the orbit, lungs and kidneys
SerologyHigh titers of antibody to U1 ribonuclear proteinIncreased serum IgG4
CourseMay evolve into classic SLE or systemic sclerosis over time. In other patients the mixture of features is maintained and steroids may offer some reliefRecently recognized in patients with extra-pancreatic manifestations of autoimmune pancreatitis, and now described in association with virtually every organ
Demographic / uncertainty—Often seen in middle-aged and older men. Pathogenesis poorly understood — it is not known whether the IgG4 antibody contributes to the pathology, and it is unclear if the disease is autoimmune at all because no target autoantigens have been identified

NICE TO KNOW The PDF is explicit that IgG4-related disease has unresolved pathogenesis. Do not assert a mechanism the lecture does not give.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Systemic sclerosis = small vessel damage plus progressive fibrosis, in women 50 to 60, more severe in African-Americans.
  • Diffuse = widespread skin, rapid, early visceral. Limited = fingers, forearms, face, late visceral, may be CREST.
  • Anti-Scl 70 → topoisomerase I → pulmonary fibrosis and peripheral vascular disease. Anti-centromere → 20 to 30% → CREST / limited.
  • Pathogenesis = autoimmunity plus vascular damage plus fibrosis, with CD4+ T cells present early.
  • Gross — mask-like face, shiny tight skin, claw hand with ulcerated fingertips. Histology — dense dermal collagen with loss of hair follicles and sweat glands.
  • MCTD → anti-U1 RNP. IgG4-RD → increased serum IgG4, obliterative phlebitis, middle-aged and older men.

19. Primary Immunodeficiency Diseases

Trans 2.02 p.7–10▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

Primary immunodeficiencies are inherited genetic defects that affect the defense mechanisms of innate immunity or the humoral and/or cellular arms of adaptive immunity. Most are detected in infancy, and the clue is susceptibility to recurrent infections.

The lecture's framing — when you hear hoof beats, people think of horses, not zebras. Doctors are taught to focus on the likeliest possibilities, but sometimes we need to look for a zebra, who are people with primary immunodeficiency.

Defects in innate immunity p.8

The inherited defects in the early innate immune response typically affect WBC functions or the complement system, and the end result is always increased susceptibility to infections.

Master table — defects in innate immunity
DiseaseGene / molecular defectConsequenceKey recall point
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1Defect in synthesis of the β chain in integrins (β chain of CD11/CD18 integrins)WBC cannot adhere to endothelium, so they cannot migrate into tissuesCD11/CD18 = LAD type 1
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2Absence of sialyl-Lewis X, the fucose-containing ligand for E and P selectinSame failure of adhesion and migrationSialyl-Lewis X = LAD type 2
Chédiak-Higashi syndromeMutation in the LYST gene, a cytosolic gene that regulates lysosomal membrane trafficDefective fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes → phagocyte dysfunction. Leukocytes contain giant granules readily seen on peripheral blood smear, thought to result from aberrant lysosome fusion. Albinism and bleeding disorders are also seenLYST plus giant granules plus albinism plus bleeding
Chronic granulomatous disease
also called Bridges-Good syndrome in the lecture figure		Inherited defects in the genes encoding components of phagocyte oxidase, the enzyme that generates superoxide. Figure names CYBA, CYBB, NCF1/2/4Defects in the bacterial killing process. The name comes from the macrophage-rich chronic inflammatory reaction that tries to control infection when the initial neutrophil defense is inadequate, which often leads to formation of granulomasNADPH / phagocyte oxidase = CGD
Complement deficienciesDescribed for all components. C2 deficiency is the most common. Figure lists C2/C4, C3, C5-9/MAC, C1 and othersC2 or C4 deficiency (early classical pathway) → increased bacterial or viral infections, though many patients have no clinical manifestations because the alternative pathway is still adequate. C3 deficiency → serious and recurrent pyogenic infections. Terminal components (needed for the MAC) → increased susceptibility to recurrent Neisseria infectionsC2 = most common. C3 = pyogenic. Terminal / MAC = Neisseria.

Defects in adaptive immunity p.8

The lecture lists seven — SCID, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, DiGeorge syndrome, common variable immunodeficiency, Hyper-IgM syndrome, isolated IgA deficiency, and X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome.

Master table — defects in adaptive immunity
DiseaseArm affected / defectClinical presentationMicroscopic / lab findingsKey recall point
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) Defective cell-mediated AND humoral response. Spans a constellation of genetically distinct syndromes all having common defects from T and B cell abnormality.
X-linked SCID — more common in males, mutation in a cytokine receptor γ-chain subunit causing loss of a transmembrane protein that is the signal transducing component of receptors for interleukins essential for survival and proliferation of T cell precursors, producing a defect at the earliest stages of T cell development.
Autosomal recessive SCID — adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, leading to accumulation of deoxyadenosine and its derivatives, toxic to rapidly dividing T lymphocytes. Several defective gene products are implicated		 Infant, severe infections, failure to thrive. Presents with prominent oral candidiasis, excessive diaper rash and failure to thrive. Infections from a wide range of pathogens — Candida albicans, P. jirovecii, Pseudomonas, cytomegalovirus, varicella and bacteria.
Without bone marrow transplantation, death often occurs in the first year of life		 X-linked — thymus with lobules of undifferentiated epithelial cells resembling fetal thymus.
Autosomal recessive — remnants of Hassall's corpuscles.
General findings for both — hypoplastic thymus and T cell areas in lymphoid tissue, with marked depletion of T cell and B cell zones		 X-linked = γ-chain. Autosomal recessive = ADA. Hassall's corpuscle remnants point to the autosomal recessive form
X-linked agammaglobulinemia
AKA Bruton's agammaglobulinemia		 No immunoglobulin or antibody production because of a failure of B cell precursors to develop into mature B cells (plasma cells), and only plasma cells can secrete antibodies.
Mechanism — during normal B cell maturation the Ig heavy chain genes rearrange first in pre-B cells, forming a complex with a surrogate light chain called the pre-B cell receptor (pre-BCR), which delivers signals inducing rearrangement of the Ig light chain genes and further maturation. This requirement is a quality control mechanism ensuring maturation proceeds only if functional immunoglobulin proteins are expressed. When the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, encoded on the long arm of the X chromosome, is mutated, maturation of B cells is arrested		 Seen almost exclusively in males (sporadic female cases possibly from mutations in other genes in the same pathway). Becomes apparent at about 6 months of age when maternal immunoglobulins are depleted. Presents with recurrent bacterial infections of the respiratory tract — Haemophilus influenzae, S. pneumoniae or S. aureus, enterovirus, and Giardia lamblia, an intestinal protozoan normally resisted by secreted IgA, which causes persistent infections.
Fungal, protozoal and intracellular viral infections are handled well by intact T-cell immunity, so they are not really a problem.
Associated diseases — arthritis and dermatomyositis in a minority		 Underdeveloped germinal centers of lymph nodes, Peyer's patches, appendix, tonsils — and plasma cells are absent BTK gene. Onset at 6 months when maternal Ig wanes. Treatment — prophylactic IV Ig therapy, which allows most individuals to reach adulthood
DiGeorge syndrome
thymic hypoplasia		 T-cell deficiency resulting from failure of development of the thymus, because the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches do not develop normally. Those pouches normally give rise to the thymus, parathyroids, some C cells and the ultimobranchial body.
Caused by a small germline deletion mapping to chromosome 22q11, so DiGeorge is now considered a component of the 22q11 deletion syndrome		 Thymic hypoplasia causing variable loss of T-cell mediated immunity, tetany from lack of parathyroids, congenital defects of the heart and great vessels, and abnormal appearance of the mouth, ears and facies Abnormally low numbers of T lymphocytes in blood and lymphoid tissues, giving poor defense against certain fungal and viral infections. Humoral immunity is also affected because T helper cells are required for B cell development 22q11. Thymus plus parathyroid plus heart plus facies
Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) Heterogeneous group of disorders whose common feature is hypogammaglobulinemia, generally affecting all antibody classes but sometimes only IgG. Some familial types show an abnormality in a receptor for BAFF, a cytokine promoting survival and differentiation of B cells, or for inducible costimulator (ICOS), though the ICOS mutation explains less than 10% of cases Clinical manifestations are similar to Bruton's agammaglobulinemia, since B cells cannot differentiate and mature into plasma cells. Both have a high frequency of autoimmune diseases, lymphoid malignancy and gastric cancer. Affects both sexes equally and the onset of symptoms is later Germinal centers and lymphoid tissues are HYPERPLASTIC, due to cells that can proliferate but are defective in further maturation. In contrast to Bruton's, most individuals with CVID have normal or near-normal numbers of B cells in blood and lymphoid tissues Hyperplastic germinal centers and normal B cell numbers separate CVID from Bruton's
Hyper-IgM syndrome Affected patients have IgM antibodies but are deficient in IgG, IgA and IgE. Many functions of CD4 helper T cells require engagement of CD40 on B cells, macrophages and dendritic cells by CD40 ligand, which induces immunoglobulin class switching and affinity maturation. Most patients have a loss-of-function mutation involving activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), a DNA-editing enzyme expressed in B cells required for Ig class switching and affinity maturation Recurrent pyogenic infections due to low levels of opsonizing IgG antibodies and impaired affinity maturation. Susceptible to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia because of defective CD40 ligand-mediated macrophage activation. Occasionally the IgM antibodies react with blood cells, giving autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia High IgM with low IgG, IgA and IgE CD40L and AID = class switching failure. IgM is stuck because switching never happens
Isolated IgA deficiency Caused by impaired differentiation of naive B lymphocytes to IgA-producing plasma cells. Molecular basis is unknown, but a defect in BAFF has been described in some patients Most individuals are asymptomatic. Because IgA is the major antibody in mucosal secretions, infections occur in the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts, and symptomatic patients present with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and diarrhea. High frequency of allergies and a variety of autoimmune diseases.
On transfusion of blood containing normal IgA, some patients develop severe, even fatal, anaphylactic reactions, because IgA behaves like a foreign antigen		 Extremely low levels of both serum and secretory IgA. Some are also deficient in the IgG2 and IgG4 subclasses Uncommon in African and Asian descent. The transfusion anaphylaxis story is the classic vignette
X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome Mutations in SLAM-associated protein (SAP), which attenuates NK cell and T cell activation, resulting in increased susceptibility to viral infections Inability to eliminate Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), leading to fulminant infectious mononucleosis and development of B-cell tumors — SAP mutation plus EBV that cannot be cleared
MUST KNOW The IgA deficiency vignette from Part 1's quiz Trans 2.01 p.11

A 35-year-old man with a history of mild upper respiratory tract infections and lifelong diarrhea who has an anaphylactic reaction after a blood transfusion has IgA deficiency. The findings indicate a failure of terminal differentiation of B cells into IgA-secreting plasma cells. Lack of IgA in mucosal secretions increases the risk of respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, and IgA antibodies present in the patient's serum can cause a transfusion reaction with the IgA in donor serum.

Immunodeficiencies associated with systemic diseases p.9–10

Comparison table — Wiskott-Aldrich vs ataxia telangiectasia
FeatureWiskott-Aldrich syndromeAtaxia telangiectasia
Triad / defining featuresThrombocytopenia, eczema, and marked vulnerability to recurrent infection resulting in early deathAbnormal gait (ataxia), vascular malformation (telangiectasia), neurologic deficits, increased incidence of tumors and immunodeficiency
Inheritance and geneX-linked recessive, mutation in the gene at Xp.11.23 encoding Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP)Autosomal recessive. Gene on chromosome 11, encoding a protein kinase called ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM)
Immune defectThymus is normal early, with progressive loss of T lymphocytes in peripheral blood and in the paracortical areas (T cell zones) of lymph nodes, and variable defects in cellular immunityDefects are of variable severity and may affect both B and T cells. T cell defects associated with thymic hypoplasia are less pronounced
Antibody picturePatients do not make antibodies to polysaccharide antigens and the response to protein antigens is poor. IgM is low, IgG is normal, and paradoxically IgA and IgE are often elevatedThe most prominent humoral abnormality is faulty production of isotype switched antibodies, mainly IgA and IgG2
MalignancyProne to develop B cell lymphomasIncreasingly frequent cancers with advancing age and a markedly increased incidence of lymphoma
OtherTreatment — hematopoietic stem cell transplantationUpper and lower respiratory tract infections, multiple autoimmune phenomena. Abnormalities in DNA repair from ATM deficiency may impair generation of antigen receptors
EXAM TRAP Similar-sounding immunodeficiencies
  • CD40 ligand → Hyper-IgM syndrome, not LAD. CD11/CD18 → LAD type 1. NADPH oxidase → CGD. LYST → Chédiak-Higashi. C5–C9 → impaired MAC formation and Neisseria infections.
  • Bruton's has ABSENT plasma cells and underdeveloped germinal centers. CVID has HYPERPLASTIC germinal centers and normal B cell numbers. Same clinical picture, opposite histology.
  • Wiskott-Aldrich paradox — IgM low, IgG normal, IgA and IgE elevated. Do not assume all isotypes fall.
  • Wiskott-Aldrich = X-linked, WASP, Xp11.23. Ataxia telangiectasia = autosomal recessive, ATM, chromosome 11.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Innate defects — LAD1 = CD11/CD18 integrins, LAD2 = sialyl-Lewis X, Chédiak-Higashi = LYST with giant granules and albinism, CGD = phagocyte (NADPH) oxidase with granulomas.
  • Complement — C2 most common, C3 → pyogenic infections, terminal MAC components → Neisseria.
  • SCID = both arms, oral candidiasis and failure to thrive, fatal in year one without bone marrow transplant. X-linked = γ-chain, autosomal recessive = ADA.
  • Bruton's = BTK, males, starts at 6 months, no plasma cells, treated with IV Ig.
  • DiGeorge = 22q11, 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, thymic hypoplasia plus tetany plus cardiac defects.
  • Hyper-IgM = CD40L and AID defect, so no class switching — high IgM, low IgG/IgA/IgE, P. jirovecii risk.
  • IgA deficiency = mostly asymptomatic, mucosal infections, and anaphylaxis to IgA-containing transfusions.
  • XLP = SAP mutation, cannot clear EBV, fulminant mononucleosis and B cell tumors.

20. Secondary / Acquired Immunodeficiency and HIV-AIDS

Trans 2.02 p.10–12▸
MUST KNOW Secondary immunodeficiency
  • More common than disorders of primary genetic origin.
  • Encountered in individuals with cancer, diabetes, malnutrition, chronic infection or renal disease, and in those receiving chemotherapy, radiation therapy or immunotherapy.
  • Can be caused by defective lymphocyte maturation when the bone marrow is damaged by radiation or chemotherapy, marrow involvement by tumors such as leukemia, inadequate immunoglobulin synthesis in malnutrition, and lymphocyte depletion from drugs or severe infections.
  • The most serious secondary immunodeficiency is AIDS.

The virus p.10

Nature of the virus
A nontransforming human retrovirus belonging to the Lentivirus family.
Cells affected
Causes depletion of CD4 T cells. Macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells are also affected.
HIV-1
US, Central Africa, Europe.
HIV-2
West Africa, India.

Infection of cells by HIV p.10

MECHANISM Entry and the co-receptor requirement
HIV gp120 binds CD4 ↓ When the virus attaches to CD4, a co-receptor called CCR5 or CXCR4 is exposed ↓ The requirement for HIV binding to co-receptors may have important implications for the pathogenesis of AIDS
  • Chemokines sterically deter HIV infection of cells in culture by occupying the receptor, so the level of chemokines in tissue may influence the efficiency of viral infection in vivo.
  • Polymorphisms in the genes encoding CCR5 are associated with different susceptibilities to HIV infection.
MUST KNOW CCR5 genetics, exact numbers p.10
Homozygous mutantAbout 1% of white Americans who inherit 2 mutant copies of the CCR5 gene are resistant to infection. Development of AIDS is associated with R5 HIV isolates.
HeterozygousAbout 20% of individuals are heterozygous for this protective CCR5 allele. They are not immune from AIDS, but the onset of their disease after infection is somewhat delayed.
Population noteOnly rare homozygotes for the mutation have been found in African and East Asian populations.

Viral replication p.10

  • Once the virus undergoes reverse transcription and the pro-viral DNA genome is inserted into the host, the virus may immediately replicate or lie dormant.
  • Replication is activated by antigen or cytokines that in turn initiate transcription factors.
  • This is the reason behind asking sexual history — co-infection with other STDs (e.g. HPV, gonorrhea) hastens viral replication by upregulating the cytokine receptors.

Mechanism of T-cell depletion p.10

1. Direct cytopathic effectLoss of infected CD4+ T cells is mainly because of the direct cytopathic effects of the replicating virus.
2. PyroptosisNon-cytopathic or abortive HIV infection activates the inflammasome pathway and leads to a pathway of cell death called pyroptosis. Inflammatory cytokines and cellular contents are released, leading to recruitment of new cells and increasing the number of cells that can be infected, which may play a role in spreading the infection.
3. Syncytia formationFusion of infected and non-infected cells may form syncytia or giant cells, which proceed to cell death within a few hours.

Natural history of HIV infection p.10–11

MECHANISM The stages in order
Initial infection starts in the mucosal tissues, because this is the point of entry of the virus. It involves memory CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells, and spreads to lymph nodes ↓ Viral replication leads to viremia and widespread seeding of lymphoid tissue ↓ Viremia is controlled by the host immune response and the patient enters a phase of clinical latency. During this time constant viral replication continues in both T cells and macrophages, but there is some form of immune containment or suppression of the virus ↓ Over time, gradual depletion of CD4+ T cells occurs until the numbers are significantly lowered and the patient develops clinical symptoms of full-blown AIDS
The immune response timeline
Comparison table — the three response curves in early HIV
ComponentTimeline and behaviorExam clue
CD4 T cellsThe body initially mounts an immune response, but CD4 T-cell numbers progressively decline as HIV disease advances — the immune system cannot keep up with the onslaughtThe falling line on the graph
Cell-mediated responseHIV-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells become detectable within the first few weeks and peak around 9 to 12 weeks. During this period HIV-specific CD8+ clones expand markedly, comprising up to 10% of CTLs at about 12 weeksCD8 peaks at 9 to 12 weeks
Humoral responseAntibody response peaks around 12 weeks. HIV tests detect antibodies against specific viral components, so there is an initial window period when a person is already infected and infectious but may still test negativeThe window period is an antibody-test problem, not an infectivity problem
MUST KNOW The single best monitoring test p.11

For clinical management, the blood CD4+ T cell count is the best and most reliable short-term indicator of disease progression. Because of this, the CD4 cell count is the primary clinical measurement used to determine when to start antiretroviral therapy (ART).

Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome — opportunistic infections p.11

  • Clinical manifestations and opportunistic infections vary in different parts of the world, and the course of the disease has been greatly modified by new ARTs, so many once-common complications became very infrequent.
  • Opportunistic infections account for the majority of deaths in untreated patients with AIDS. Many represent reactivation of latent infections that are normally kept in check by a robust immune system but are not completely eradicated because these infectious agents have evolved to coexist with their hosts.

Common pathogens listed — cryptosporidiosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, mycobacteriosis (typical and atypical), nocardiosis, JC virus, CMV, HSV, VZ.

Master table — the specific opportunistic infections the lecture details
InfectionKey detailNumbers to keep
Pneumonia caused by the fungus P. jiroveciiWas the presenting feature in about 20% of cases. Incidence is much less in patients who respond to ART20% presenting feature
Oral thrush / oral candidiasisIn asymptomatic HIV-infected individuals it is a sign of immunologic decompensation and often heralds transition to AIDSThe transition marker
Cryptosporidium (protozoan) or Isospora belliCause the persistent diarrhea common in untreated advanced AIDS. Diarrhea in AIDS is chronic, profuse and watery with massive fluid lossChronic, profuse, watery
Cytomegalovirus (CMV)May cause disseminated disease or be localized to the eye or GIT. CMV chorioretinitis was seen in approximately a quarter of patients but its incidence has decreased dramatically due to ARTOccurs almost exclusively at CD4 count under 50 cells/µL

Clinical features of AIDS — neoplasms and CNS p.11

Neoplasms — all caused by oncogenic DNA viruses
  • Kaposi sarcoma → Human Herpesvirus 8
  • B cell lymphoma → EBV
  • Cervical and anal cancer → HPV

Viruses may establish latent infections even in healthy people, but they are usually suppressed by a competent immune system.

CNS involvement
  • AIDS dementia complex
  • Meningitis, encephalitis, peripheral neuropathies
  • 90% of patients demonstrate some form of neurologic involvement at autopsy
  • More than half have clinically apparent neurologic dysfunction
  • Neurologic manifestations may be the sole or earliest presenting feature in some patients

Rates of progression p.11

Without treatment, most patients progress to AIDS after a chronic phase lasting 7 to 10 years, with three exceptions.

Comparison table — the three progression patterns
GroupDefinitionNumbers
Rapid progressorsMiddle or chronic phase is shortened2 to 3 years after primary infection
Long term non-progressorsUntreated HIV-1-infected individuals who remain asymptomatic for 10 years or more, with very stable CD4+ T cell counts and low plasma viremia5 to 15% of infected individuals. Viremia usually less than 500 RNA copies/mL
Elite controllersA small percentage with undetectable virus. There is evidence of a vigorous anti-HIV immune response in all cases, though the immune correlates of protection are still unknown. Some have high levels of HIV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses maintained over the course of infection, and inheritance of particular HLA alleles also seems to correlate with resistance to disease progression, reflecting the ability to mount antiviral T-cell responsesUnder 50 to 75 RNA copies/mL

Combination antiretroviral drug therapy (ART) p.11–12

MUST KNOW What ART does and does not do
  • The lecture's quote — a combination of at least three effective drugs in a motivated, compliant patient reduces HIV replication below the level of detection (under 50 copies RNA per mL) and keeps it there indefinitely.
  • ART only suppresses the virus and does NOT eradicate or kill it.
  • Treated patients still carry viral DNA in their lymphoid tissues and can infect other individuals.
  • Second and third line ART are already on the market for breakthrough infections or when the disease becomes resistant to the initial treatment.
Benefits, IRIS and side effects
  • Reduced transmission of virus, especially from infected mothers to newborns.
  • Decreased opportunistic infections.
  • Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) — patients with advanced disease given ART have a paradoxical deterioration in their clinical condition as the immune system recovers, from a poorly regulated host response to the high antigenic burden of persistent microbes.
  • Side effects — lipoatrophy (loss of facial fat), lipoaccumulation (excessive fat deposition in the central areas of the body), lipodystrophy (changes in fat distribution often accompanied by metabolic abnormalities), elevated lipids, insulin resistance and peripheral neuropathy.
EXAM TRAP Obstacles to a vaccine

Viral variation makes vaccine and antibody development difficult. Therefore prevention, public health measures and antiretroviral therapy remain the mainstays of AIDS control — not vaccination.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Secondary immunodeficiency is more common than primary, and AIDS is the most serious.
  • HIV is a nontransforming retrovirus of the Lentivirus family that depletes CD4 T cells and also affects macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells.
  • gp120 binds CD4, exposing CCR5 or CXCR4. 2 mutant CCR5 copies in about 1% of white Americans = resistance, heterozygous in about 20% = delayed onset only.
  • T cell depletion — direct cytopathic effect (main), pyroptosis via the inflammasome, and syncytia formation.
  • Infection starts in mucosal tissue → viremia and lymphoid seeding → clinical latency with ongoing replication → CD4 depletion → AIDS.
  • CD8 response peaks at 9 to 12 weeks, antibody peaks around 12 weeks, leaving a window period.
  • CD4 count is the best short-term indicator and decides when to start ART.
  • KS → HHV-8. B cell lymphoma → EBV. Cervical and anal cancer → HPV. 90% have neurologic involvement at autopsy.
  • Untreated course is 7 to 10 years. Rapid = 2 to 3 years, long-term non-progressors = 5 to 15%, elite controllers = undetectable.
  • ART suppresses but does not eradicate, patients remain infectious, and IRIS is a paradoxical worsening as immunity recovers.

21. Transplant Rejection and Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant

Trans 2.02 p.12–14▸
MUST KNOW Why the kidney is the model

Most of the pathology in transplant rejection has been studied in the kidneys because it is the most transplanted organ. Before transplanting any organ, many barriers must be overcome because of the immune reaction brought about by T and B cells, so we must ensure that the blood type and the tissue of the donor and recipient match.

A. Tests done for kidney transplant p.12

Blood typing
Done in order to avoid type I and II hypersensitivity reactions. Incompatible blood results in anaphylactic shock.
Tissue typing
Checks HLA / MHC incompatibility. The major antigenic differences between donor and recipient that result in rejection are due to differences in HLA alleles. HLA genes are highly pleomorphic, resulting in differences between individuals, except in identical twins.
Cross matching
Tests the recipient's serum for antibodies against the donor's cells. Any detected mismatch will prompt the recipient's T and B cells to recognize the donor's organ as foreign and begin to destroy it.

B. Pathways of transplant recognition p.12

Following transplantation, the recipient's T cells recognize donor HLA antigens from the graft by two pathways — direct and indirect.

Direct pathway
  • T cells of the recipient recognize donor MHC molecules on the surface of APCs in the graft
  • APCs in the donated tissue express high levels of Class 1 and Class 2 molecules and are also endowed with costimulatory molecules
  • Host T cells encounter the donor dendritic cells either within the grafted organ or after the dendritic cells migrate to the lymph nodes
  • CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize Class 1 MHC and differentiate into active cytotoxic T cells
  • CD4+ helper T cells recognize Class 2 MHC and proliferate and differentiate into effector cells
  • Allogeneic MHC molecules with their bound peptides resemble or mimic the self MHC–foreign peptide complexes recognized by self MHC-restricted T cells. In other words, recognition of allogeneic MHC is a cross reaction of T cells selected to recognize self MHC plus foreign peptides
  • This pathway plays a greater role in CTL-mediated ACUTE rejection of organ transplants
Indirect pathway
  • Recipient T lymphocytes recognize MHC antigens of the graft donor AFTER they are presented by the recipient's own APC
  • Peptides derived from the donor tissue are presented by the host's own MHC molecules like any other foreign peptide
  • It is similar to the physiologic processing and presentation of other foreign antigens
  • This pathway plays a greater role in CHRONIC rejection of organ transplants
EXAM TRAP Direct vs indirect and what they cause

Direct = donor APC presents on donor MHC = acute, CTL-mediated rejection. Indirect = recipient APC presents donor peptide on recipient MHC = chronic rejection. The word "direct" refers to whose MHC is doing the presenting, not to speed — although it does happen to pair with the acute reaction.

C. Mechanisms of transplant recognition p.12–13

Master table — the five rejection reactions by mechanism
RejectionMediatorTimingMechanismKey recall point
Acute cellular rejection T cell mediated — T cells and antibodies activated by antigens in the graft Within days or weeks after transplantation. Appears much later if immunosuppression is tapered or terminated CD4+ helper T cells secrete cytokines and induce inflammation, which damages the graft. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly destroy the graft cells and may also react against graft vessels, leading to vascular damage Principal cause of EARLY graft failure
Chronic rejection T cell mediated Over months or years, an indolent form of graft damage Manifests as interstitial fibrosis and graft arteriosclerosis. In both lesions the culprits are T cells that react against graft alloantigens and secrete cytokines, which stimulate proliferation and activity of fibroblasts and vascular smooth muscle cells Progressive loss of graft function. Fibrosis plus arteriosclerosis
Hyperacute rejection B cell mediated — preformed donor antibodies already present in the recipient's circulation Within minutes or hours Preformed antibody attacks immediately Sensitized individuals — a recipient who has already rejected a transplanted organ, or a multiparous woman who developed antibodies against paternal HLA antigens shed from the fetus. Not considered a significant problem today because of the current practice of cross-matching blood
Acute antibody-mediated rejection B cell mediated — antibodies produced AFTER transplantation Acute Exposure to the Class 1 and Class 2 HLA antigens of the donor graft and the antigens that differ between donor and recipient invokes antibodies. These may cause complement-dependent cytotoxicity, inflammation, and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity The initial target of these antibodies is the GRAFT VASCULATURE
Chronic antibody-mediated rejection B cell mediated Develops insidiously (gradually) without preceding acute rejection Affects vascular components. Antibodies are detected in the circulation but are not readily identified within the graft. Mechanism of the vascular lesions is not well understood A slow and steady rise in creatinine may be the only clue that the organ is being rejected

D. Rejection reactions in the kidney — morphology p.13

1. Hyperacute rejection
  • Occurs within minutes or hours after transplantation.
  • Gross — the kidney becomes rapidly cyanotic, mottled and flaccid, and may excrete only a few drops of bloody urine.
  • Immunoglobulin and complement are deposited into the vessel wall, causing endothelial injury and fibrin-platelet thrombi.
  • Microscopic — neutrophils rapidly accumulate in the arterioles, glomeruli and peritubular capillaries. As changes become more diffuse and intense, the glomeruli undergo thrombotic occlusion of the capillaries, and fibrinoid necrosis occurs in the arterial walls.
EXAM TRAP The classic rejection vignette

A transplanted kidney biopsy showing abundant neutrophils within arterioles, glomeruli and peritubular capillaries is hyperacute rejection — not acute cellular and not acute humoral. The Part 1 answer key explains — hyperacute rejection is caused by preformed antibodies against the donor graft, leading to classical complement activation, C4d deposition, endothelial injury and thrombosis, and the presence of neutrophils in glomeruli and peritubular capillaries supports antibody-mediated vascular injury. Trans 2.01 p.10–11

2. Acute cellular rejection (T-cell mediated) — two patterns
Tubulointerstitial pattern (Type 1)
  • Extensive interstitial inflammation with lymphocytic infiltration of the tubular epithelium — tubulitis
  • Associated with focal tubular injury
Endothelitis (Type 2)
  • Vascular pattern showing inflammation of vessels, sometimes with fibrinoid necrosis (Type 3)
  • Lymphocytes can be seen between the endothelium and vessel wall
  • A normal blood vessel's lumen is patent, while the pathologic vessel's lumen is occluded and filled with proliferating smooth muscle cells
MUST KNOW Why recognizing cellular rejection matters p.13
  • In the absence of accompanying humoral rejection, patients respond well to immunosuppressive therapy, which preserves the transplanted organ.
  • Giving certain drugs that control the actions of the T cells ensures the longevity of the transplanted organ.
  • If the antibody or humoral type of rejection is involved, it is difficult to remove these antibodies, since they are more widely spread in the body.
3. Acute antibody-mediated rejection
  • Mainly manifested by damage to the glomeruli and small blood vessels.
  • Lesions typically consist of inflammation of the glomeruli and peritubular capillaries, and small vessels may show focal thrombosis.
  • Associated deposition of the complement breakdown product C4d is highlighted by immunoperoxidase stain. C4d is produced during activation of the complement system by the classical pathway, and it deposits in peritubular capillaries and glomeruli.
4. Chronic rejection
  • Patients present clinically with progressive renal failure, manifested by a rise in serum creatinine over a period of 4 to 6 months.
  • Dominated by vascular changes — intimal thickening with inflammation, and glomerulopathy with duplication of the basement membrane and peritubular capillaritis.
  • Interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy with loss of renal parenchyma, which may occur secondary to the vascular lesions.

E. Methods of increasing transplant / graft survival p.13

HLA matching
  • Between donor and recipient
  • A 100% compatible organ would have to match 12 HLA alleles, which is difficult unless they are identical twins
Immunosuppressive therapy
  • Certain drugs suppress the immune reaction to increase graft survival
  • Prolongs the graft but carries risks — increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections, mostly viruses
MUST KNOW Viral complications of immunosuppression p.13
  • One of the most frequent infectious complications is reactivation of Polyoma virus. It establishes latent infection in the lower genitourinary tract of healthy individuals, and upon immunosuppression it is activated and can infect the renal tubules and cause graft failure.
  • Reactivation of other latent viral infections due to diminished host defenses can also cause Epstein-Barr virus-induced lymphoma, HHV-8-associated Kaposi sarcoma, and Human papilloma virus-induced squamous cell carcinoma.

F. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant p.13–14

  • Indications are usually confined to diseases of the blood — leukemia, aplastic anemia, immunodeficiency states, thalassemia.
  • Stem cell transplants for solid cancers like breast cancer or colon cancer have NOT been found to be helpful.
  • In most conditions where it is indicated, the recipient is irradiated or treated with high doses of chemotherapy, which destroys the immune cells and opens up a niche in the marrow microenvironment to allow the transplanted cells to engraft and repopulate the entire bone marrow.
MECHANISM Procedure of hematopoietic stem cell transplant, in strict order
1. Collection — stem cells are harvested from the patient's bone marrow or blood ↓ 2. Processing — the stem cell product or bone marrow is processed to concentrate the stem cells ↓ 3. Cryopreservation — the processed product is frozen to preserve it ↓ 4. Chemotherapy — the patient receives high-dose chemotherapy or radiation therapy ↓ 5. Infusion — thawed stem cells or bone marrow are infused back into the patient

Two problems are seen in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation — graft vs host disease (GVHD) and immunodeficiency.

Graft vs host disease (GVHD) p.14

MUST KNOW Core definition

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically crippled recipients. The transferred cells recognize antigens in the host and attack the host tissue. Because recipients are immunosuppressed, the graft attacks the recipient rather than the other way round. Immunocompetent T cells of the donor recognize the recipient's HLA antigens as foreign and react against them. To minimize this reaction, HLA alleles in recipient and donor have to match.

Comparison table — acute vs chronic GVHD
FeatureAcute GVHDChronic GVHD
OnsetWithin days to weeks after bone marrow transplantOccurs insidiously (gradually) or may follow the acute syndrome
SkinGeneralized rash, and in severe cases a diffuse rash leading to desquamationExtensive cutaneous injury with destruction of the skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, which may mimic systemic sclerosis
LiverJaundice caused by destruction of small bile ductsChronic liver disease manifested by cholestatic jaundice (frequent)
GITBloody diarrhea caused by mucosal ulceration of the gutDamage may cause esophageal strictures and fibrosis
LymphoidAlthough tissue injury may be severe, affected tissues are usually NOT infiltrated or heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. In addition to direct cytotoxicity of CD8+ T cells, damage is inflicted by cytokines released by the sensitized donor T cellsInvolution of the thymus (common) and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes (common)
Other—Patients may experience recurrent and life-threatening infections, and some may develop a form of autoimmunity as a result of the donor's CD4+ helper T cells reacting with the host's B cells, stimulating them to produce antibodies
EXAM TRAP The counter-intuitive GVHD histology

In acute GVHD, tissue injury may be severe yet the affected tissues are usually NOT heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes, because much of the damage comes from cytokines released by sensitized donor T cells rather than from a visible cellular infiltrate. A bland biopsy does not rule out severe GVHD.

COMMON CONFUSION Transplant rejection vs GVHD
Transplant rejection

Host attacks the graft. Recipient T and B cells recognize donor HLA. Target = the transplanted organ.

Graft vs host disease

Graft attacks the host. Donor T cells recognize recipient HLA, which is possible because the recipient is immunosuppressed. Targets = skin, liver and GIT.

HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Three pre-transplant tests — blood typing, tissue typing (HLA/MHC), cross matching.
  • MHC is the major molecule recognized as foreign in transplantation, and T cells recognize donor MHC through their TCRs, initiating rejection.
  • Direct pathway → acute CTL-mediated rejection. Indirect pathway → chronic rejection.
  • Hyperacute = minutes to hours, preformed antibody, neutrophils in glomeruli and peritubular capillaries, fibrin-platelet thrombi, fibrinoid necrosis.
  • Acute cellular = days to weeks, principal cause of early graft failure, patterns tubulitis (Type 1) and endothelitis (Type 2), and it responds well to immunosuppression if there is no humoral component.
  • Acute antibody-mediated targets the graft vasculature and shows C4d by immunoperoxidase.
  • Chronic = months to years, creatinine rise over 4 to 6 months, interstitial fibrosis plus graft arteriosclerosis.
  • 100% HLA match needs 12 alleles. Immunosuppression invites Polyoma virus reactivation causing graft failure, plus EBV lymphoma, HHV-8 Kaposi sarcoma and HPV squamous cell carcinoma.
  • GVHD = graft attacks host, targets skin, liver and GIT, and chronic GVHD can mimic systemic sclerosis.

22. Amyloidosis

Trans 2.02 p.14–15▸
MUST KNOW Core definition

Amyloidosis is the build up of pathologic proteinaceous material in tissues and organs — a condition associated with a number of inherited and inflammatory disorders in which misfolded and abnormal fibrillar proteins are deposited extracellularly. These proteins are insoluble and become responsible for functional compromise and tissue damage because the body cannot clear them away.

Classification p.14

Systemic / generalized
  • Primary — associated with plasma cell disorders
  • Secondary — occurs as a complication of an underlying chronic inflammation or tissue destructive process
Localized

Limited to a single organ or tissue.

Hereditary / familial

A separate heterogeneous group with its own distinctive patterns of organ involvement.

A. Amyloid proteins p.14

Misfolded proteins are normally degraded intracellularly or extracellularly by macrophages. In amyloidosis these quality control mechanisms fail, leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins outside the cells.

Normal proteins

Have a tendency to fold improperly when produced in increased or abnormal amounts. Examples — AL protein, AA protein.

Mutant proteins

Are prone to misfolding and aggregation when produced in NORMAL amounts. Example — ATTR protein.

Master table — the amyloid proteins
ProteinCategoryAssociated conditionDistributionKey recall point
Amyloid Light (AL) protein Normal protein made in abnormal amounts Occurs in plasma cell disorders associated with amyloidosis like multiple myeloma Systemic All cases are caused by clonal proliferation of neoplastic plasma cells that synthesize an immunoglobulin prone to form amyloid, due to its unique physio-chemical properties
Amyloid-Associated (AA) protein Normal protein made in abnormal amounts Reactive systemic amyloidosis. Previously referred to as secondary amyloidosis, because it is secondary to an associated inflammatory condition. Prior to effective antimicrobial therapy, TB and chronic osteomyelitis were the most important underlying conditions, and nowadays these are hardly seen — it is now more commonly seen in autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and inflammatory bowel disease Amyloid is deposited systemically The "chronic inflammation" amyloid
Serum Amyloid-Associated (SAA) protein Precursor of AA In reactive systemic amyloidosis, solid tumors such as renal cell carcinoma and some kinds of lymphoma can result in amyloidosis Systemic Produced by liver cells during inflammation. Long standing inflammation results in sustained elevation of SAA levels. However increased production of SAA by itself is not sufficient for amyloid deposition — the individual's unique genetic makeup plays a role
Mutant transthyretin (ATTR) Mutant protein misfolding at normal amounts Transthyretin is a normal serum protein that binds and transports thyroxine and retinol. Mutant forms and its fragments are deposited in a group of genetically-determined disorders called familial amyloid polyneuropathies Familial, and also cardiac in the elderly Senile systemic amyloidosis — the mutant form and at times the NORMAL transthyretin can be deposited in the heart of elderly individuals
EXAM TRAP The elderly heart failure vignette

A 79-year-old man with worsening congestive heart failure, pulmonary and peripheral edema, cardiomegaly with four-chamber dilation, and NORMAL serum protein electrophoresis and bone marrow smear has senile cardiac amyloidosis from deposition of TRANSTHYRETIN — not IgE, calcitonin or β2-microglobulin. The normal electrophoresis and marrow are what rule out the plasma cell (AL) type. Trans 2.01 p.10–11

B. Morphology — gross features p.14

Grossly, deposited amyloid enlarges the organ.

Sago spleen
  • Amyloid deposits appear as numerous gray-white nodules on the surface of the organ
  • Nodules have the consistency of sago
  • They appear as nodules because the amyloid is deposited in the SPLENIC FOLLICLES
Lardaceous spleen
  • Deposits are found in the splenic SINUSOIDS and surrounding connective tissue
  • Gives the organ a greasy or lard-like consistency

Morphology — microscopic features p.15

Diagnosis of this disease ultimately depends on morphologic identification of amyloid.

Comparison table — the three microscopic methods, in the order you use them
MethodWhat amyloid looks likeWhy you use it
Light microscopy with H&E stainAmorphous eosinophilic hyaline extracellular substanceFirst look, but it cannot separate amyloid from other hyaline material
Congo Red stainPink or red color in the tissue depositsMost commonly used method to differentiate amyloid from other hyaline material such as collagen
Polarizing microscopyGreen birefringence of the stained amyloidConfirms the Congo Red finding
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY
  • Amyloid = misfolded fibrillar protein deposited EXTRACELLULARLY, insoluble, and not clearable.
  • Normal proteins misfold when overproduced (AL, AA). Mutant proteins misfold at normal amounts (ATTR).
  • AL → plasma cell disorders / multiple myeloma. AA → chronic inflammation, now mostly RA, ankylosing spondylitis and IBD. SAA is the liver-made precursor of AA. ATTR → familial amyloid polyneuropathies and senile cardiac amyloidosis.
  • Sago spleen = nodular, follicles. Lardaceous spleen = greasy, sinusoids.
  • H&E = amorphous eosinophilic hyaline. Congo Red = pink-red. Polarized light = green birefringence.

23. Commonly Confused Concepts COMMON CONFUSION

Both lessons▸

Every pair below is drawn only from the two lectures. The last column is the one-line distinction to say out loud before you answer.

Do not confuse — defining feature, key clue, fast distinction
Do not confuseA — defining featureB — defining featureFast distinction
Innate vs adaptive immunityInnate — present before infection, non-specific, no memory, pattern recognition onlyAdaptive — learned, specific, needs prior exposure, more potentAsk whether sensitization is required. If no, it is innate
PAMPs vs DAMPsPAMPs — shared microbial structures necessary for infectivityDAMPs — molecules from injured and necrotic cells (also expressed by transformed malignant cells)Pathogen vs damage. Tumor cells express DAMPs
MHC class I vs class IIClass I — all nucleated cells and platelets, cytosolic/viral/tumor peptides, read by CD8Class II — mainly APCs, HLA-D region, endosomal/lysosomal peptides, read by CD4The product equals 8 — 1×8 and 2×4
NK cell vs cytotoxic T cellNK — innate, no TCR, no antigen response, CD16 → ADCC, kills cells lacking MHC ICTL — adaptive, TCR, MHC class I restricted, kills with perforin and granzymeMissing self kills by NK. Presented self kills by CTL.
Mast cell vs eosinophil in type IMast cell — responsible for most symptoms, immediate phase, granule mediatorsEosinophil — dominant cell of the late phase, major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein, Charcot-Leyden crystalsMinutes = mast cell. 2 to 24 hours = eosinophil.
Immediate vs late phase reactionImmediate — minutes, vascular plus smooth muscle, vasodilation-congestion-edema, urticariaLate — 2 to 24 hours, sustained inflammation, cellular infiltrate, asthma, continues without further allergenFluid change vs cell influx
Type II vs type III hypersensitivityType II — antibody binds antigen fixed on a cell surface or in the ECMType III — preformed circulating Ab–Ag complexes deposit in vessel walls, kidney, skin and jointsWhere was the antigen when the antibody found it? On a cell = II. In the blood = III
Type III immunofluorescence vs type II (Goodpasture)Type III — granular, lumpy deposits of immunoglobulin and complementType II against basement membrane binds a continuous structure, so staining is smooth and linearLumpy = landed complexes. Linear = antibody against the membrane itself.
Myasthenia gravis vs Graves diseaseMG — antibody BLOCKS the ACh receptor at the motor end plate → muscle weaknessGraves — antibody STIMULATES the TSH receptor → hyperthyroidismSame type II arm (cellular dysfunction), opposite direction
Serum sickness vs Arthus reactionSerum sickness — systemic prototype, single large antigen exposure, resolves by catabolism of complexesArthus — local, skin, antigen diffuses into the vessel wall and meets preformed antibody, causing fibrinoid necrosisSystemic vs local, and Arthus needs preformed antibody
Th1 vs Th17 in type IVTh1 — IFN-γ and TNF, inflammation dominated by activated macrophagesTh17 — IL-17 and IL-22, inflammation with a greater neutrophil componentMacrophage-heavy = Th1. Neutrophil-heavy = Th17.
Central vs peripheral toleranceCentral — thymus and bone marrow, negative selection / clonal deletion and receptor editing, with AIREPeripheral — elsewhere, anergy, Treg suppression (IL-10 and TGF-β), deletion by apoptosis, with PD-1 and CTLA-4Central deletes before release. Peripheral catches escapees.
Anergy vs deletion by apoptosisAnergy — the cell survives but is unresponsive because signal 2 never cameDeletion — the self-reactive cell receives signals promoting death and diesAlive but silent vs dead
Anti-Scl 70 vs anti-centromereAnti-Scl 70 — DNA topoisomerase I, pulmonary fibrosis and peripheral vascular disease, diffuse systemic sclerosisAnti-centromere — 20 to 30% of patients, CREST / limited presentationScl-70 is NOT the CREST antibody — the lecture quiz marks that pairing wrong
Lupus nephritis class III vs IVClass III focal — less than 50% of glomeruliClass IV diffuse — 50% or more, most common and severe, wire-loops, cellular crescentsThe lesions are identical, only the extent differs
Lupus nephritis class IV vs class VClass IV — subendothelial deposits → wire-loop capillary wallsClass V membranous — subepithelial deposits → silver-stain spikes, severe proteinuria and nephrotic syndromeWhich side of the basement membrane the deposit sits on
Bruton's agammaglobulinemia vs CVIDBruton's — BTK, males, starts at 6 months, plasma cells absent, underdeveloped germinal centersCVID — both sexes equally, later onset, HYPERPLASTIC germinal centers, normal or near-normal B cell numbersClinically similar. Histology is opposite.
LAD type 1 vs type 2LAD 1 — β chain of CD11/CD18 integrinsLAD 2 — absence of sialyl-Lewis X, the fucose ligand for E and P selectinIntegrin vs selectin ligand
Chédiak-Higashi vs chronic granulomatous diseaseChédiak-Higashi — LYST, defective phagosome-lysosome fusion, giant granules, albinism, bleedingCGD — phagocyte (NADPH) oxidase, CYBA / CYBB / NCF1-2-4, granulomasFusion failure vs killing failure
Primary vs secondary APASPrimary — hypercoagulable state without SLE or other autoimmune disorder, idiopathicSecondary — in association with SLE, acquired from an underlying diseaseIs there an underlying autoimmune disease or not
Direct vs indirect transplant recognitionDirect — recipient T cells read donor MHC on donor APCs → acute CTL-mediated rejectionIndirect — recipient APCs present donor peptides on recipient MHC → chronic rejectionWhose MHC presents it decides the pathway, and the pathway decides acute vs chronic
Hyperacute vs acute cellular vs acute antibody-mediated rejectionHyperacute — minutes to hours, preformed antibody, neutrophils in arterioles, glomeruli and peritubular capillaries, thrombi, fibrinoid necrosisAcute cellular — days to weeks, T cell, tubulitis or endothelitis. Acute antibody-mediated — antibody made after transplant, targets graft vasculature, C4d positivePreformed vs newly formed antibody vs T cells
Transplant rejection vs GVHDRejection — host attacks graftGVHD — graft attacks host, possible because the recipient is immunosuppressed. Targets skin, liver, GITWho is doing the attacking
AL vs AA vs ATTR amyloidAL — plasma cell disorder / multiple myeloma, a normal protein made in abnormal amountsAA — chronic inflammation (RA, ankylosing spondylitis, IBD), precursor is liver-made SAA. ATTR — mutant transthyretin at normal amounts, familial polyneuropathies and senile cardiac amyloidosisPlasma cells vs inflammation vs mutation
Sago vs lardaceous spleenSago — gray-white nodules, amyloid in the splenic folliclesLardaceous — greasy, lard-like, amyloid in the sinusoids and surrounding connective tissueFollicles make lumps. Sinusoids make grease.

24. Exam Traps EXAM TRAP

Both lessons▸

Details that flip an answer. All are stated in the two lectures or their own answer keys.

Opposite effects on the same receptor

ACh receptor antibody blocks → myasthenia gravis, weakness. TSH receptor antibody stimulates → Graves, hyperthyroidism. Do not let "antireceptor antibody" push you to one answer.

Which complement pathway

Type II opsonization activates the CLASSICAL pathway. Chymase and tryptase in type I activate the ALTERNATIVE pathway, and only because of the resulting tissue injury. C4d in transplant rejection is a classical pathway product.

The cytokine that sits in both columns

IFN-γ is listed under BOTH innate and adaptive in Table 1. Use TNF, IL-1, IL-12 and type I IFNs for innate, and IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-17, TGF-β and IL-10 for adaptive.

Nickel patch test cytokine

Focal erythema and induration 24 to 48 hours after nickel exposure with itching and pain and recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes → the cytokine is IL-17 from the TH17 subset. Not IL-5, IL-10 or IL-12.

Reduced MHC class I on an infected cell

If viral transformation reduces MHC class I, the killer is the natural killer cell, not CD4, macrophage or dendritic cell. NK inhibitory receptors stop receiving their negative signal, so the cell is killed. NK cells are often the first line of defense against viral infection.

Two signals, and what one signal gives you

Signal 1 alone (TCR without co-stimulation) produces ANERGY, not suppression, apoptosis or self tolerance as a separate answer. Anergy is also the basis of tumor tolerance.

Checkpoint inhibitor colitis

Severe colitis after pembrolizumab is type IV, T cell-mediated. It is not type I, because there is no mast cell degranulation in severe colitis. Managed with corticosteroids.

Pembrolizumab's exact target

PD-1 on T cells binding PD-L1 on tumor cells. Not CD28–B7, not Fas–Fas ligand, not MHC II–CD4.

Lupus anticoagulant is a misnomer

PTT is prolonged in vitro but patients are HYPERCOAGULABLE in vivo — thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage, cerebral or ocular ischemia. It can also give a false positive syphilis serology.

Least specific ANA pattern

Speckled is frequently observed, making it the least specific pattern. Homogeneous → SLE. Nucleolar and centromeric → systemic sclerosis. Speckled → Sjögren in this table.

Autoimmune antibody pairings

From the lecture quiz — the correct pair is inflammatory myopathy with Jo-1 (histidyl-tRNA synthetase, polymyositis / dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome). Wrong pairs — CREST with Scl-70, drug induced SLE with anti-DNA and anti-Sm, Sjögren with anti-centromere.

Drug induced vs subacute cutaneous LE

Drug induced → anti-HISTONE and HLA-DR4. Subacute cutaneous → SS-A and HLA-DR3. Chronic discoid → anti-dsDNA rarely present.

HLA-B27 is an association, not a cause

100 to 200-fold greater chance of ankylosing spondylitis, yet the presence of the HLA gene itself is not the cause of the disease.

Neutrophils in a transplanted kidney

Abundant neutrophils within arterioles, glomeruli and peritubular capillaries = HYPERACUTE rejection. Preformed antibody, classical complement, C4d, endothelial injury and thrombosis.

Wiskott-Aldrich immunoglobulin paradox

IgM low, IgG normal, and paradoxically IgA and IgE often ELEVATED. Patients cannot make antibodies to polysaccharide antigens and respond poorly to protein antigens.

Complement deficiency by level

C2 is the most common deficiency. C2 or C4 may be clinically silent because the alternative pathway suffices. C3 → serious recurrent pyogenic infections. Terminal / MAC components → recurrent Neisseria.

IgA deficiency and transfusion

Most patients are asymptomatic, but transfusion of blood containing normal IgA can cause severe, even fatal anaphylaxis because IgA behaves like a foreign antigen. Also uncommon in African and Asian descent.

Bruton's timing

Becomes apparent at about 6 months of age, when maternal immunoglobulins are depleted — not at birth.

ART does not cure

ART only suppresses the virus and does NOT eradicate or kill it. Treated patients still carry viral DNA in lymphoid tissues and can infect others, even at under 50 copies/mL.

CCR5 heterozygotes are not protected

2 mutant copies → resistance (about 1% of white Americans). Heterozygous (about 20%) are NOT immune — only the onset is somewhat delayed.

IRIS looks like treatment failure

Patients with advanced disease given ART can have a paradoxical deterioration as the immune system recovers, from a poorly regulated response to a high antigenic burden. Worsening on ART is not automatically drug failure.

Acute GVHD can look bland

Tissue injury may be severe yet the tissues are usually NOT heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes, because much of the damage is cytokine-mediated.

Senile cardiac amyloid

Elderly heart failure with normal serum protein electrophoresis and normal bone marrow → transthyretin, not a plasma cell (AL) process.

Congo Red is the discriminator

H&E only tells you there is amorphous eosinophilic hyaline material. Congo Red is what separates amyloid from collagen and other hyaline material, confirmed by green birefringence under polarized light.

Type III deposits where blood is filtered

Medium-sized complexes in slight antigen excess are the most pathogenic, and they deposit where blood is filtered at high pressure to form urine and synovial fluid — hence glomeruli and joints. Not simply "wherever blood flows fastest."

Stem cell transplant indications

Confined to diseases of the blood — leukemia, aplastic anemia, immunodeficiency states, thalassemia. Stem cell transplants for solid cancers like breast or colon cancer have NOT been found helpful.

25. CRAM SHEET — the 5 to 10 minute full run-through

Both lessons, no new information▸

Eighteen unlock-everything items. If you only have ten minutes left, read this section alone from top to bottom.

1. The two immune systems, as a key-value card

Innate
Present before infection. Non-specific, no memory, no sensitization needed. Barriers, phagocytes, mast cells, NK cells, complement. Logic = recognize → activate → eliminate.
Adaptive
Learned, specific, more potent, needs prior antigen exposure. T cells = cell mediated = intracellular. B cells = humoral = extracellular.
Pattern recognition
PAMPs from microbes plus DAMPs from injured, necrotic and malignant cells, read by 4 receptor classes.

2. The four pattern recognition receptors, as a grid

TLRPlasma membrane and endosome. Cytoplasmic → NF-κB → cytokines and adhesion molecules. Endosomal → interferon regulatory factors → antiviral cytokines.
NLRCytosolic. Inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1, which recruits neutrophils and induces fever.
CLRMacrophages and DCs. Fungal glycans → anti-fungal inflammation.
RLRCytosol of most cells. Nucleic acids of cytoplasmic viruses → antiviral cytokines.

3. MHC, as a contrast block plus the mnemonic

Class I → CD8
  • All nucleated cells and platelets
  • Cytosolic, viral and tumor peptides
  • CD8 binds the heavy chain
  • Exists everywhere because virus and cancer can start in any cell
Class II → CD4
  • Mainly APCs — B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells
  • HLA-D region
  • Endosomal and lysosomal peptides
  • Present ingested antigen and respond to helper T signals
From the PDF

1 × 8 = 8 and 2 × 4 = 8. HLA genes sit on chromosome 6. Only identical twins share MHC, which is why transplants are rejected.

4. Cytokine pairings, as a rapid table

CytokineActionCytokineAction
IL-1Neutrophils plus feverIL-12NK killing plus IFN-γ secretion
IL-2T cell growth factor, NK proliferationIL-13Enhances IgE production
IL-4IgE class switching plus more Th2IL-15NK proliferation (with IL-2)
IL-5Activates eosinophilsIL-17Recruits neutrophils and monocytes
IFN-γPotent macrophage activatorIL-10 and TGF-βTreg suppressive cytokines

5. Antibody isotypes, as plain facts

  • IgG and IgM activate complement. IgA is mucosal. IgE arms mast cells and eosinophils. IgM or IgD is the B cell antigen receptor.
  • Only plasma cells secrete antibodies. Polysaccharides and lipids drive mainly IgM and are T-independent.

6. The four hypersensitivity types, as one master table

TypeMediatorLesionPrototype
I ImmediateIgE on mast cells, driven by Th2Vascular dilation, edema, smooth muscle contraction, mucusAnaphylaxis, allergy, atopic asthma
II Antibody-mediatedIgG / IgM against cell surface or ECMPhagocytosis and lysis, inflammation, or functional derangement without injuryAutoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture
III Immune complexDeposited Ab–Ag complexesNecrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosisSLE, serum sickness, Arthus
IV Cell-mediatedCD4+ T cells (Th1 and Th17), plus CTLsPerivascular infiltrates, granuloma, cell destructionContact dermatitis, MS, type 1 diabetes, TB
From the PDF — ACID

Atopy/Allergy, Cytotoxic antibody, Immune complex, Delayed.

7. Type I timeline, as an arrow chain

Allergen → APC in epithelial barrier → naive CD4 → Th2 ↓ IL-4 and IL-13 B cell IgE class switching → IgE binds mast cell receptors = sensitization ↓ repeat exposure Mast cell degranulation ├── vasoactive amines and lipid mediators → immediate reaction, minutes, urticaria └── cytokines → late phase, 2 to 24 hours, eosinophils, asthma, continues without further allergen

Histamine does three things — smooth muscle contraction, vascular permeability, mucus secretion. Atopy = increased serum IgE plus strong family history. Injection such as a bee sting → systemic anaphylaxis.

8. Type II, as a numbered mechanism plus its diseases

  1. Antibody binds the cell
  2. Complement activation (classical pathway)
  3. C3b / C4b opsonization
  4. Phagocytosis, or MAC with osmotic lysis, or ADCC

Three arms — opsonization and phagocytosis, antibody-mediated inflammation (basement membrane and ECM, causing glomerulonephritis and graft vascular rejection), and antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction (myasthenia gravis blocks, Graves stimulates). Drug reactions use a hapten on the RBC membrane. Erythroblastosis fetalis = maternal IgG across the placenta.

9. Type III, as three phases plus a deposition rule

Complex formation→ Deposition in vessels→ Acute inflammation and tissue injury

Medium-sized complexes in slight antigen excess are most pathogenic, depositing where blood is filtered at high pressure → glomeruli and joints. Morphology = acute necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis and intense neutrophils, kidney IF = granular lumpy, EM = electron-dense deposits along the GBM. Serum sickness is systemic, Arthus is local. Autoimmune diseases named — SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, membranous glomerulonephritis.

10. Type IV, as a branching mechanism

Persistent antigen presented to CD4+ T cell ├── Th1 → IFN-γ and TNF → activated macrophages → epithelioid cells → multinucleated giant cells → granuloma rimmed by lymphocytes └── Th17 → IL-17 and IL-22 → neutrophil-rich inflammation CTL route → perforin and granzymes kill tissue cells directly

PPD is the classic example — reddening and induration within 72 hours. Morphology = perivascular cuffing by mononuclear cells, mainly CD4+.

11. Immunity in cancer, as a contrast block

Innate
  • No sensitization, no immediate response, no memory
  • Recognizes DAMPs on transformed cells
  • NK cells kill "missing self" tumor cells lacking MHC I
  • IL-12 and TNF-α recruit more innate cells
Adaptive
  • MHC II → CD4 → IFN-γ and IL-2 help
  • MHC I → CD8 → perforin then granzymes then caspases then apoptosis
  • Signal 1 (TCR-MHC) plus signal 2 (B7-CD28). Signal 1 alone = anergy = tumor tolerance
  • Humoral arm mostly in breast cancer and lymphoma

Evasion — PD-L1 up, MHC I loss, Tregs/MDSCs, TGF-β. CTLA-4 and PD-L1 are the key tolerance checkpoints. Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1/PD-L1, and its cost is colitis, thyroiditis and pneumonitis, treated with corticosteroids.

12. Tolerance, as a two-column card

Central — thymus and bone marrow
  • Negative selection / clonal deletion by apoptosis, helped by AIRE which puts tissue-restricted self-antigens in the thymus
  • Receptor editing in B cells, or apoptosis if editing fails
  • Cells that do not recognize self can become Tregs
  • Not foolproof
Peripheral — everywhere else
  • Anergy — signal 1 without signal 2, reinforced by PD-1 and CTLA-4, the brakes
  • Suppression by Tregs via IL-10 and TGF-β
  • Deletion by apoptosis

13. Causes of autoimmunity, as plain bullets

  • Susceptibility genes plus an environmental trigger.
  • HLA-B27 and ankylosing spondylitis — 100 to 200-fold risk, yet the gene is not the cause.
  • Infection acts by inducing costimulators on APCs (breaking anergy) and by molecular mimicry, prototype rheumatic heart disease.
  • EBV and HIV → polyclonal B cell activation. UV light exposes nuclear antigens in lupus. More common in women.
  • Autoimmune disease is chronic, relapsing-remitting, progressive, with no cure.

14. SLE, as a compressed table

DomainWhat to remember
HallmarkAntinuclear antibodies. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are virtually diagnostic. Injury by immune complex deposition
WhoWomen 17 to 55, peak 20s to 30s, 2 to 3 fold higher in Blacks and Hispanics
CriteriaSLICC — 4 criteria including at least one clinical and one immunologic, revised 2012
ANA patternsHomogeneous → SLE. Speckled → Sjögren, least specific. Nucleolar and centromeric → systemic sclerosis
APASAbout 40%. Prolonged PTT in vitro, hypercoagulable in vivo — thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage, cerebral or ocular ischemia. Cross-reacts with syphilis serology
GeneticsHLA-DQ. C1q, C2 or C4 deficiency impairs clearance of complexes
SkinMalar rash in half. Microscopy = vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer, edema at the dermo-epidermal junction, IgG along the dermoepidermal junction on IF
KidneyI minimal mesangial (IF/EM only) · II mesangial proliferative · III focal, under 50% · IV diffuse, 50% or more, most common and severe, WIRE-LOOPS · V membranous, subepithelial, spikes, nephrotic · VI over 90% sclerosis, end stage
HeartLibman-Sacks — 1 to 3 mm warty deposits on any surface of any valve
VariantsChronic discoid — skin only, anti-dsDNA rare. Subacute cutaneous — SS-A, HLA-DR3. Drug induced — anti-histone, HLA-DR4, from hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, D-penicillamine

15. The other autoimmune diseases, as a matrix

Rheumatoid arthritisAutoantibodies against citrullinated peptides. ACPAs are the diagnostic markers. Rheumatoid factor is IgM and IgA against the Fc portion of IgG. Joints and blood vessels.
Sjögren syndromeDry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) plus dry mouth (xerostomia), from destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands. SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La) in up to 90%. Parotid enlargement in half. Biopsy = lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration with ductal epithelial hyperplasia. 5% get marginal zone lymphoma, 40-fold increase.
Systemic sclerosisVascular damage plus progressive fibrosis, women 50 to 60. Diffuse = widespread skin, early visceral. Limited = fingers, forearms, face, late visceral, CREST. Anti-Scl 70 = topoisomerase I, pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-centromere = 20 to 30%, CREST. Gross = mask-like face, claw hand, ulcerated fingertips. Histology = dense dermal collagen with loss of hair follicles and sweat glands.
MCTD and IgG4-related diseaseMCTD — overlaps SLE, scleroderma and polymyositis, high titer anti-U1 RNP. IgG4-RD — IgG4 plasma cells, fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, raised serum IgG4, middle-aged and older men, pathogenesis still unresolved.

16. Immunodeficiencies, as one master table

DiseaseDefectSignature clue
LAD type 1β chain of CD11/CD18 integrinsCannot adhere to endothelium
LAD type 2Absence of sialyl-Lewis XSelectin ligand missing
Chédiak-HigashiLYST geneGiant granules, albinism, bleeding
Chronic granulomatous diseasePhagocyte (NADPH) oxidase — CYBA, CYBB, NCF1/2/4Granulomas when neutrophil killing fails
ComplementC2 most commonC3 → pyogenic. Terminal / MAC → Neisseria.
SCIDX-linked = cytokine receptor γ-chain. Autosomal recessive = ADA deficiencyOral candidiasis, diaper rash, failure to thrive. Death in year 1 without bone marrow transplant. Hassall's corpuscle remnants in the ADA form
Bruton's agammaglobulinemiaBTK on the long arm of XMales, onset at 6 months, plasma cells absent, treated with IV Ig. Giardia lamblia persists
DiGeorge22q11 deletion, 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouchesThymic hypoplasia, tetany, cardiac and great vessel defects, abnormal facies
CVIDHypogammaglobulinemia, BAFF or ICOS receptor abnormalityHyperplastic germinal centers, normal B cell numbers, both sexes, later onset
Hyper-IgMCD40 ligand and AIDHigh IgM, low IgG/IgA/IgE. P. jirovecii pneumonia
Isolated IgA deficiencyImpaired differentiation to IgA-producing plasma cellsUsually asymptomatic, mucosal infections, anaphylaxis to IgA-containing transfusion
X-linked lymphoproliferativeSAP mutationCannot clear EBV → fulminant mononucleosis and B cell tumors
Wiskott-AldrichWASP, Xp11.23, X-linked recessiveThrombocytopenia, eczema, infections. IgM low, IgG normal, IgA and IgE elevated
Ataxia telangiectasiaATM, chromosome 11, autosomal recessiveAtaxia, telangiectasia, tumors. Faulty isotype-switched IgA and IgG2

17. HIV and AIDS, as a highlight box

  • Nontransforming retrovirus, Lentivirus family. HIV-1 in US, Central Africa, Europe. HIV-2 in West Africa, India.
  • gp120 binds CD4, exposing CCR5 or CXCR4. Two mutant CCR5 copies in about 1% of white Americans = resistance. Heterozygous about 20% = delayed onset only.
  • T cell loss by direct cytopathic effect (main), pyroptosis via the inflammasome, and syncytia formation.
  • Course — mucosal entry → viremia and lymphoid seeding → clinical latency with continuing replication → CD4 depletion → AIDS. CD8 peaks at 9 to 12 weeks, antibody around 12 weeks, leaving a window period.
  • CD4 count is the best short-term indicator and decides when to start ART.
  • Opportunistic — P. jirovecii was the presenting feature in about 20%, oral thrush heralds transition to AIDS, Cryptosporidium diarrhea is chronic, profuse and watery, CMV retinitis almost only at CD4 under 50 cells/µL.
  • Tumors — KS from HHV-8, B cell lymphoma from EBV, cervical and anal cancer from HPV. 90% have neurologic involvement at autopsy.
  • Untreated course 7 to 10 years. Rapid progressors 2 to 3 years. Long term non-progressors 5 to 15%, viremia under 500 copies/mL. Elite controllers under 50 to 75 copies/mL.
  • ART = at least three drugs, suppresses below 50 copies/mL but does NOT eradicate, patients stay infectious. IRIS = paradoxical worsening as immunity recovers. Side effects include lipoatrophy, lipoaccumulation, lipodystrophy, elevated lipids, insulin resistance, peripheral neuropathy.

18. Transplant rejection and amyloidosis, as two compact tables

RejectionTimingMediator and signature
HyperacuteMinutes to hoursPreformed antibody. Cyanotic mottled flaccid kidney, few drops of bloody urine, neutrophils in arterioles, glomeruli and peritubular capillaries, fibrin-platelet thrombi, fibrinoid necrosis
Acute cellularDays to weeksT cells. Principal cause of early graft failure. Type 1 tubulointerstitial = tubulitis. Type 2 endothelitis. Type 3 adds fibrinoid necrosis. Responds well to immunosuppression if no humoral component
Acute antibody-mediatedAcute, antibody formed after transplantTargets the graft vasculature. C4d by immunoperoxidase in peritubular capillaries and glomeruli
ChronicMonths to yearsCreatinine rise over 4 to 6 months. Interstitial fibrosis and graft arteriosclerosis, intimal thickening, glomerulopathy with basement membrane duplication
GVHDAcute = days to weeks. Chronic = insidiousGraft attacks host. Acute — rash, jaundice from bile duct destruction, bloody diarrhea, and tissues usually NOT heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. Chronic — mimics systemic sclerosis, cholestatic jaundice, esophageal strictures, thymic involution

Pathways — direct → acute CTL rejection, indirect → chronic rejection. Three tests — blood typing, tissue typing, cross matching. A 100% match needs 12 HLA alleles. Immunosuppression invites Polyoma virus reactivation causing graft failure, plus EBV lymphoma, HHV-8 Kaposi sarcoma and HPV squamous cell carcinoma.

AmyloidSourceClue
ALClonal neoplastic plasma cells, e.g. multiple myelomaNormal protein, abnormal amount. Systemic
AA (precursor SAA)Chronic inflammation — historically TB and osteomyelitis, now RA, ankylosing spondylitis, IBD. SAA is made by liver cells during inflammationRaised SAA alone is not enough — genetic makeup matters
ATTRMutant transthyretin at normal amountsFamilial amyloid polyneuropathies and senile systemic (cardiac) amyloidosis in the elderly

Gross — sago spleen = nodules, amyloid in the follicles. Lardaceous spleen = greasy, amyloid in the sinusoids. Microscopy — H&E amorphous eosinophilic hyaline → Congo Red pink-red → polarized light green birefringence.

26. RAPID-FIRE FINAL RECALL — 100 prompts

Both lessons · answers hidden▸

Say the answer out loud, then open the prompt to check. Every answer comes from the two lectures.

Part 1 — basic immunity, cells, MHC, cytokines

1. Three-step logic of innate immunity?
Recognize → activate → eliminate.
2. Two limitations of innate immunity?
It is not specific — it can only produce inflammation, not antibodies — and it has no memory, so it cannot respond faster on second exposure.
3. Source of PAMPs vs DAMPs?
PAMPs are structures shared among related microbes, often necessary for infectivity. DAMPs are molecules released by injured and necrotic cells.
4. The 4 classes of pattern recognition receptors?
Toll-like, Nod-like, C-type lectin, Rig-like.
5. Transcription factor activated by cytoplasmic TLR, and what it makes?
NF-κB, which stimulates synthesis and secretion of cytokines and expression of adhesion molecules — both needed for leukocyte recruitment and activation.
6. NLR signaling chain down to the cytokine?
Inflammasome → caspase-1 → cleaves the precursor of IL-1. IL-1 recruits neutrophils and induces fever.
7. Which receptor detects fungal glycans, and on which cells?
C-type lectin receptors, on the plasma membrane of macrophages and dendritic cells.
8. Two ways NK cells differ from T lymphocytes?
They do not have T-cell receptors and they do not respond to antigens.
9. Most important role of the dendritic cell?
Present antigens to other cells to initiate T cell responses, because DCs express high levels of MHC and other molecules needed for antigen presentation and T cell activation. It also links adaptive and innate immunity.
10. Which two opsonins do macrophages read?
IgG and C3b.
11. NK cell receptor for ADCC, and the cytokines that regulate NK activity?
CD16, conferring the ability to lyse IgG-coated targets. IL-2 and IL-15 stimulate proliferation. IL-12 activates killing and IFN-γ secretion.
12. Microscopic description of a plasma cell?
Eccentric nucleus with a checkerboard appearance and a paranuclear hoof or clearing beside the nucleus. A mature small lymphocyte by contrast is 6 to 9 micrometers with a dense homogeneous nucleus almost filling the cell.
13. Chromosome carrying HLA genes, and where on it?
Chromosome 6, on a small segment of the short arm.
14. Which cells express MHC class I, and which express class II?
Class I — all nucleated cells and platelets. Class II — mainly antigen-presenting cells, namely B lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells.
15. Why must every nucleated cell carry MHC class I?
Because viral infection and cancer may both arise from any nucleated cell, so all nucleated cells must be surveyable by CD8⁺ T cells.
16. Two signals needed for full T cell activation?
TCR recognition of the antigen–MHC complex, plus a co-stimulatory signal such as CD28 (binding B7). TCR recognition alone is not sufficient.

Part 1 — hypersensitivity and cancer

17. The ACID mnemonic?
Atopy and allergy (I), Cytotoxic antibody-mediated (II), Immune complex deposition (III), Delayed-type (IV).
18. Main mechanism of type I hypersensitivity?
A rapid reaction in a previously sensitized individual triggered by binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells.
19. Three actions of histamine?
Intense smooth muscle contraction, increased vascular permeability, stimulation of mucus secretion.
20. IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 in type I?
IL-4 stimulates IgE class switching in B cells and promotes more Th2 cells. IL-5 activates eosinophils. IL-13 enhances IgE production.
21. Dominant cell of the late phase, and its damaging products?
Eosinophil. Major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein damage tissues, and Charcot-Leyden crystals promote inflammation and enhance TH2 responses.
22. Onset and classic association of the immediate vs late phase?
Immediate — within minutes, urticaria / hives, with vasodilation, congestion and edema. Late — 2 to 24 hours, asthma, with an inflammatory cellular infiltrate, and it continues even without continuous allergen exposure.
23. Two features of atopic individuals?
Increased serum IgE and a strong family history of allergies or asthma.
24. The hygiene hypothesis in one line?
