Early childhood exposure to certain microorganisms builds the immune system and may protect against allergic disease, while lack of exposure impairs development of immune tolerance and predisposes to allergies.
25. Four steps of the type II mechanism?
Antibody binds cell → complement activation → C3b/C4b opsonization → phagocytosis, or MAC formation, or ADCC.
26. Which type II arm causes no tissue injury, and its two examples?
Antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction, which targets cell-surface receptors and does not necessarily cause tissue injury or inflammation. Examples — myasthenia gravis (ACh receptor blocked) and Graves disease (TSH receptor stimulated).
27. Which immune complexes are most pathogenic, and where do they deposit?
Medium-sized Ab/Ag complexes formed under conditions of slight antigen excess. They concentrate where blood is filtered at high pressure to form urine and synovial fluid, so disease often affects glomeruli and joints.
28. Principal morphologic manifestation of immune complex injury?
Acute vasculitis, with necrosis of the blood vessel and intense neutrophilic infiltration, appearing as a smudgy eosinophilic area of tissue destruction termed fibrinoid necrosis.
29. Systemic vs local prototype of type III?
Acute serum sickness is the systemic prototype. The Arthus reaction is the local one — a localized area of tissue necrosis from acute immune complex vasculitis, often in the skin, with fibrinoid necrosis in vessel walls.
30. Three autoimmune diseases that use the type III mechanism?
Systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa, membranous glomerulonephritis.
31. Th1 vs Th17 inflammation in type IV?
Th1-associated inflammation is dominated by activated macrophages. Th17-triggered inflammation has a greater neutrophil component.
32. Classic example of delayed type hypersensitivity, and the timing?
The tuberculin (PPD) skin test, by intradermal or intracutaneous injection of purified protein derivative. In a sensitized person, reddening and induration appear within 72 hours then slowly subside.
33. Sequence from persistent antigen to granuloma?
Persistent or non-degradable antigen → T cell cytokines → sustained macrophage activation → epithelioid cells (large, abundant cytoplasm) → multinucleated giant cells → granuloma surrounded by lymphocytes.
34. Signal 1 without signal 2 produces what, and why does it matter in cancer?
Anergy, which is the basis of tumor tolerance.
35. Drug of choice named in the lecture for checkpoint blockade, its target, and its cost?
Pembrolizumab, which blocks PD-1/PD-L1 to release the brakes on exhausted CD8+ T cells. Its cost is immune-related adverse events from loss of peripheral tolerance — colitis, thyroiditis and pneumonitis — managed with corticosteroids.

Part 2 — tolerance, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, HIV, transplant, amyloid

36. Mechanisms of central tolerance for T and for B cells, and the gene that helps?
T cells — negative selection (clonal deletion) with killing by apoptosis in the thymus, assisted by AIRE, which stimulates expression of peripheral tissue-restricted self-antigens in the thymus. B cells — receptor editing in the bone marrow, with apoptosis if editing fails.
37. Three mechanisms of peripheral tolerance, and the Treg cytokines?
Anergy, suppression by regulatory T cells, deletion by apoptosis. Tregs secrete IL-10 and TGF-β, which inhibit lymphocyte activation and effector functions.
38. Two immune checkpoint molecules named as the brakes?
PD-1 and CTLA-4, receptors structurally homologous to CD28.
39. Risk conferred by HLA-B27, and the caveat?
A 100 to 200-fold greater chance of ankylosing spondylitis, but the presence of the HLA gene itself is not the cause of the disease.
40. Two mechanisms linking infection to autoimmunity, with the classic mimicry example?
Induction of costimulators on APCs, which breaks anergy, and molecular mimicry. The example is rheumatic heart disease, where antibodies against streptococcal proteins cross-react with myocardial proteins.
41. Hallmark of SLE and the two virtually diagnostic antibodies?
Hallmark is production of antinuclear antibodies. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm (Smith) antigen are virtually diagnostic.
42. The four ANA fluorescence patterns and their diseases?
Homogeneous → dsDNA and nuclear envelope proteins → SLE. Speckled → non-DNA constituents such as Sm, ribonucleoprotein, SS-A and SS-B → Sjögren, and it is the least specific pattern. Nucleolar → RNA → systemic sclerosis. Centromeric → centromeres → systemic sclerosis.
43. Why is "lupus anticoagulant" a misnomer?
Because although the antibodies interfere with in vitro clotting tests like the PTT, patients actually have complications of excessive clotting and are in a hypercoagulable state — venous and arterial thrombosis, recurrent spontaneous miscarriage, focal cerebral or ocular ischemia.
44. What is an LE cell?
A phagocytic leukocyte that has engulfed the denatured nucleus of an injured cell. In vivo, nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern and become homogeneous, forming LE bodies or hematoxylin bodies.
45. Which complement deficiencies predispose to SLE, and by what mechanism?
Deficiencies of C1q, C2 or C4, which impair removal of circulating immune complexes, favoring tissue deposition.
46. Microscopic skin findings in SLE?
Vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer of the epidermis, variable edema at the dermo-epidermal junction with perivascular inflammation in the dermis, prominent vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis, and on immunofluorescence deposition of immunoglobulin and complement along the dermoepidermal junction.
47. Which class of lupus nephritis is most common and severe, and its light-microscopic signature?
Class IV, diffuse lupus nephritis, affecting half or more of the glomeruli. Subendothelial deposits cause circumferential capillary wall thickening forming wire-loop structures, and epithelial proliferation produces cellular crescents filling Bowman's space.
48. Class V and class VI lupus nephritis in one line each?
Class V membranous — diffuse capillary wall thickening from subepithelial deposits with silver-stain spikes, usually with severe proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. Class VI advanced sclerosing — sclerosis of more than 90% of glomeruli, representing end-stage renal disease.
49. Describe Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
Nonbacterial verrucous or warty endocarditis with single or multiple 1 to 3 mm warty deposits on any surface of the leaflet of any heart valve. It used to be common before the widespread use of steroids.
50. Antibody and HLA association of drug induced lupus, and the drugs?
Antibodies specific for histone, associated with HLA-DR4. Drugs — hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid and D-penicillamine.
51. Autoantibodies of rheumatoid arthritis, and what rheumatoid factor targets?
Autoantibodies specific for citrullinated peptides (CCPs), in which arginine residues are converted to citrulline, detected as anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs). Rheumatoid factor is IgM and IgA directed against the Fc portion of IgG.
52. Two serologic markers of Sjögren syndrome and their detection rate?
Antibodies against the ribonucleoprotein antigens SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La), detectable in as many as 90% of patients.
53. Lip or salivary gland biopsy finding in Sjögren, and why dry mouth results?
Intense lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration with ductal epithelial hyperplasia. The duct is obstructed with no lumen for saliva to pass through, producing xerostomia.
54. Malignancy risk in Sjögren syndrome?
About 5% develop marginal zone lymphoma, an incidence 40-fold greater than normal individuals.
55. CREST syndrome, and which antibody goes with it?
Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. It goes with anti-centromere antibody, found in 20 to 30% of patients and with the limited presentation.
56. What does anti-Scl 70 target and predict?
It is directed against DNA topoisomerase I, and those patients are more likely to have pulmonary fibrosis and peripheral vascular diseases.
57. The three interrelated processes of systemic sclerosis, and the gross picture?
Autoimmunity, vascular damage and fibrosis — that is, T and B cell activation plus vascular damage plus collagen deposition. Gross — blank mask-like face, shiny smooth tightly drawn skin, lips pressed together, claw deformity of the hands with ulcerated fingertips.
58. Histologic findings in systemic sclerosis skin, and why the skin looks shiny?
Extensive deposition of dense collagen in the dermis with virtual absence of hair follicles and sweat glands and foci of inflammation. The absence of hair follicles and sweat glands is what makes the skin shiny and smooth.
59. Antibody in mixed connective tissue disease?
High titers of antibody to U1 ribonuclear protein, in a disease overlapping SLE, scleroderma and polymyositis.
60. Defects in LAD type 1 vs type 2?
Type 1 — defect in synthesis of the β chain in integrins (CD11/CD18). Type 2 — absence of sialyl-Lewis X, the fucose-containing ligand for E and P selectin. Without these the WBC cannot adhere to endothelium or migrate into tissues.
61. Gene and blood smear finding in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?
Mutation in the LYST gene, which regulates lysosomal membrane traffic, causing defective fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes. Leukocytes contain giant granules readily appreciated on peripheral blood smear. Albinism and bleeding disorders are also seen.
62. Enzyme defective in chronic granulomatous disease, and why granulomas form?
Phagocyte oxidase (NADPH oxidase), the enzyme that generates superoxide, from mutations in CYBA, CYBB or NCF1/2/4. Granulomas form because a macrophage-rich chronic inflammatory reaction tries to control the infection when the initial neutrophil defense is inadequate.
63. Most common complement deficiency, and which deficiency predisposes to Neisseria?
C2 is the most common. Deficiency of the terminal components, required for assembly of the membrane attack complex, gives increased susceptibility to recurrent Neisseria infections. C3 deficiency gives serious recurrent pyogenic infections.
64. The two genetic forms of SCID and their defects?
X-linked SCID — mutation in a cytokine receptor γ-chain subunit, losing the signal transducing component of receptors for interleukins essential for survival and proliferation of T cell precursors. Autosomal recessive SCID — adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, with accumulation of deoxyadenosine and derivatives toxic to rapidly dividing T lymphocytes.
65. Gene, timing and histology of Bruton's agammaglobulinemia?
Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) on the long arm of the X chromosome. Becomes apparent at about 6 months of age, when maternal immunoglobulins are depleted. Histology — underdeveloped germinal centers of lymph nodes, Peyer's patches, appendix and tonsils, with plasma cells absent. Treatment is prophylactic IV Ig therapy.
66. Embryologic and genetic basis of DiGeorge syndrome, and its four clinical features?
The 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches do not develop normally, from a small germline deletion at chromosome 22q11. Features — thymic hypoplasia with variable loss of T-cell immunity, tetany from lack of parathyroids, congenital defects of the heart and great vessels, and abnormal mouth, ears and facies.
67. Two histologic findings that separate CVID from Bruton's?
In CVID the germinal centers and lymphoid tissues are hyperplastic, and B cell numbers in blood and lymphoid tissue are normal or near-normal. In Bruton's, germinal centers are underdeveloped and plasma cells are absent.
68. Immunoglobulin profile and the two molecular defects in Hyper-IgM syndrome?
IgM present but deficient IgG, IgA and IgE. Defects are in CD40 ligand engagement of CD40, and a loss-of-function mutation in activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), the DNA-editing enzyme needed for class switching and affinity maturation.
69. Why can isolated IgA deficiency cause fatal anaphylaxis?
On transfusion of blood containing normal IgA, some patients develop severe, even fatal anaphylactic reactions, because IgA behaves like a foreign antigen.
70. Defect and consequence in X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome?
Mutations in SLAM-associated protein (SAP), which attenuates NK and T cell activation, so patients cannot eliminate EBV, leading to fulminant infectious mononucleosis and B-cell tumors.
71. Wiskott-Aldrich triad, gene, and immunoglobulin pattern?
Thrombocytopenia, eczema, and marked vulnerability to recurrent infection. X-linked recessive mutation at Xp11.23 encoding WASP. IgM low, IgG normal, and paradoxically IgA and IgE often elevated, with no antibodies to polysaccharide antigens. Treatment — hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
72. Gene and chromosome in ataxia telangiectasia?
A protein kinase called ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), encoded on chromosome 11, autosomal recessive. Faulty production of isotype switched antibodies, mainly IgA and IgG2.
73. HIV family, and which co-receptors are exposed after CD4 binding?
A nontransforming human retrovirus of the Lentivirus family. gp120 binds CD4, exposing CCR5 or CXCR4.
74. CCR5 genetics — homozygous and heterozygous?
About 1% of white Americans inherit 2 mutant copies and are resistant to infection. About 20% are heterozygous — they are not immune, but onset of disease after infection is somewhat delayed.
75. Three mechanisms of CD4 T cell depletion in HIV?
Direct cytopathic effects of the replicating virus (the main one), pyroptosis from non-cytopathic or abortive infection activating the inflammasome pathway, and fusion of infected and non-infected cells forming syncytia or giant cells that die within a few hours.
76. Best short-term indicator of HIV disease progression, and what it decides?
The blood CD4+ T cell count, which is the primary clinical measurement used to determine when to start antiretroviral therapy.
77. Peak times of the CD8 and antibody responses, and what the gap causes?
HIV-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells peak around 9 to 12 weeks, comprising up to 10% of CTLs at about 12 weeks. Antibody response peaks around 12 weeks. Because tests detect antibodies, there is an initial window period when a person is infected and infectious but may still test negative.
78. Four AIDS-associated tumors and their viruses?
Kaposi sarcoma → human herpesvirus 8. B cell lymphoma → EBV. Cervical and anal carcinoma → HPV. All are oncogenic DNA viruses.
79. CD4 threshold for CMV chorioretinitis, and the presenting opportunistic infection in about 20% of cases?
CMV chorioretinitis occurs almost exclusively at CD4 counts under 50 cells/µL. Pneumonia caused by the fungus P. jirovecii was the presenting feature in about 20% of cases.
80. Define rapid progressors, long term non-progressors and elite controllers.
Rapid progressors — chronic phase shortened to 2 to 3 years after primary infection. Long term non-progressors — 5 to 15% of infected individuals, asymptomatic for 10 years or more, stable CD4 counts, viremia usually under 500 RNA copies/mL. Elite controllers — undetectable virus, under 50 to 75 RNA copies/mL.
81. What does ART achieve and what does it not achieve?
At least three effective drugs reduce replication below 50 copies RNA per mL indefinitely in a compliant patient. But it only suppresses and does not eradicate or kill the virus — patients still carry viral DNA in lymphoid tissues and can infect other individuals.
82. What is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome?
Patients with advanced disease given ART have a paradoxical deterioration in clinical condition as the immune system recovers, from a poorly regulated host response to the high antigenic burden of persistent microbes.
83. Three tests done before a kidney transplant?
Blood typing (to avoid type I and II hypersensitivity, since incompatible blood results in anaphylactic shock), tissue typing for HLA/MHC incompatibility, and cross matching, which tests the recipient's serum for antibodies against the donor's cells.
84. Direct vs indirect pathway, and which rejection each drives?
Direct — recipient T cells recognize donor MHC on APCs in the graft, and it plays a greater role in CTL-mediated acute rejection. Indirect — recipient T cells recognize donor MHC antigens after presentation by the recipient's own APC on the host's MHC, and it plays a greater role in chronic rejection.
85. Timing and microscopic findings of hyperacute rejection?
Minutes to hours. The kidney becomes rapidly cyanotic, mottled and flaccid and may excrete only a few drops of bloody urine. Microscopically, neutrophils rapidly accumulate in arterioles, glomeruli and peritubular capillaries, with thrombotic occlusion of glomerular capillaries and fibrinoid necrosis of arterial walls, following deposition of immunoglobulin and complement in the vessel wall.
86. Two patterns of acute cellular rejection?
Tubulointerstitial pattern (Type 1) — extensive interstitial inflammation with lymphocytic infiltration of tubular epithelium, called tubulitis, with focal tubular injury. Endothelitis (Type 2) — inflammation of vessels with lymphocytes between the endothelium and vessel wall, sometimes with fibrinoid necrosis (Type 3), and the lumen occluded by proliferating smooth muscle cells.
87. Stain and marker for acute antibody-mediated rejection?
Deposition of C4d, highlighted by immunoperoxidase stain, in peritubular capillaries and glomeruli. C4d is produced during classical pathway complement activation. The initial target is the graft vasculature.
88. Clinical and morphologic picture of chronic rejection?
Progressive renal failure with a rise in serum creatinine over 4 to 6 months. Dominated by vascular changes — intimal thickening with inflammation and glomerulopathy with duplication of the basement membrane and peritubular capillaritis, plus interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy.
89. How many HLA alleles must match for a 100% compatible organ, and which virus most frequently reactivates under immunosuppression?
12 HLA alleles, difficult unless the donor and recipient are identical twins. Polyoma virus reactivation is one of the most frequent infectious complications — it is latent in the lower genitourinary tract and can infect the renal tubules and cause graft failure.
90. Five steps of hematopoietic stem cell transplant?
Collection → processing → cryopreservation → chemotherapy (or radiation) → infusion.
91. Definition of GVHD and its three acute target organs?
It occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically crippled recipients, and donor T cells recognize the recipient's HLA antigens as foreign. Acute targets — skin (generalized rash, desquamation), liver (jaundice from destruction of small bile ducts), GIT (bloody diarrhea from mucosal ulceration).
92. Which autoimmune disease does chronic GVHD mimic?
Systemic sclerosis, because of extensive cutaneous injury with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis.
93. Definition of amyloidosis?
A condition associated with inherited and inflammatory disorders in which misfolded and abnormal fibrillar proteins are deposited extracellularly. They are insoluble and cause functional compromise and tissue damage because the body cannot clear them away.
94. AL, AA and SAA protein — what underlies each?
AL — clonal proliferation of neoplastic plasma cells synthesizing an amyloid-prone immunoglobulin, as in multiple myeloma, systemic distribution. AA — reactive systemic amyloidosis secondary to chronic inflammation, historically TB and chronic osteomyelitis, now more commonly RA, ankylosing spondylitis and IBD. SAA — the precursor of AA, produced by liver cells during inflammation, but raised SAA alone is not sufficient for deposition.
95. Which protein is deposited in senile systemic amyloidosis, and what is its normal job?
Transthyretin, a normal serum protein that binds and transports thyroxine and retinol. The mutant form and at times the normal transthyretin can be deposited in the heart of elderly individuals. Mutant forms also cause familial amyloid polyneuropathies.
96. Sago vs lardaceous spleen?
Sago spleen — numerous gray-white nodules with the consistency of sago, because amyloid is deposited in the splenic follicles. Lardaceous spleen — deposits in the splenic sinusoids and surrounding connective tissue, giving a greasy or lard-like consistency.
97. The three-step microscopic diagnosis of amyloid?
H&E shows an amorphous eosinophilic hyaline extracellular substance. Congo Red turns the deposits pink or red and is the most commonly used method to differentiate amyloid from other hyaline material such as collagen. Polarizing microscopy shows green birefringence.
98. Which stem cell transplant indications are useful, and which are not?
Useful — diseases of the blood — leukemia, aplastic anemia, immunodeficiency states, thalassemia. Not helpful — solid cancers such as breast cancer or colon cancer.
99. Major molecule responsible for rejection of a transplanted organ?
MHC. MHC molecules are the major molecules recognized as foreign during transplantation, and T cells recognize donor MHC (alloantigens) through their T-cell receptors, which initiates the rejection response.
100. Which cell responds when viral transformation reduces MHC class I on an infected cell, and why?
The natural killer cell. NK cells carry receptors for MHC class I that inhibit their lytic function, so when class I expression is reduced the inhibitory receptors receive no negative signal and the cell is killed. NK cells are often the first line of defense against viral infection and need no prior sensitization.
